meta.title: Trump in Texas, 13 days of posts
meta.subject: President Donald Trump's role in Texas politics — endorsements and rallies for Ken Paxton, Greg Abbott and Dan Patrick, attacks on James Talarico and Gina Hinojosa, federal actions affecting Texas, and how Texas voters and candidates invoke him before the Nov 3, 2026 election
meta.subtitle: Oct 6 to Oct 18, 2026. Each dot is one post with 1K+ views about Trump and Texas, plus every post repeating an earlier one, in the lane for what it argues. Higher and bigger means more views. White means 90% or more the same words as an earlier post, with a white line back to it. Coloured lines link a post to the post it quoted or replied to. Updated daily.

lanes.label: Trump rally shows Texas loyalty
lanes.description: Trump's San Antonio rally and surrogate appearances (Vance, Cruz) prove huge crowds, enthusiasm and a firm Trump-Paxton-Abbott ticket, with the media forced to concede Texas is still red.

lanes.label: Talarico freak, vegan, missing
lanes.description: Trump and allies attack James Talarico as weak, fake, a 'vegan' or 'Talafreako', claim he went missing for nearly two weeks, hint at a mental health stay, and demand medical records and a debate with Paxton.

lanes.label: Trump dragging down Texas GOP
lanes.description: Trump's war, gas prices and chaotic events are hurting Paxton and Republicans, shown by Paxton's leaked audio, protesters repeatedly disrupting the rally, and rally flubs read as a sign of decline.
keywords: so much for that paxton boost

lanes.label: Texas slipping: polls show tight race
lanes.description: Polls and forecasts showing Paxton and Abbott tied or trailing Talarico and Hinojosa, with flip predictions and below-2024 Trump margins, are cited as evidence Texas is turning purple or blue, or alternatively as a race still within Paxton's reach.

lanes.label: Paxton scandals and Trump's choice
lanes.description: Paxton's scandals, the Trump endorsement over Cornyn, and his refusal to debate Talarico are framed as a weak, compromised candidate Trump chose despite warnings.

lanes.label: Trump administration actions in Texas
lanes.description: Federal actions affecting Texas are cast either as affordability and security wins (Defense Production Act refinery in Tyler, Trump Accounts, border enforcement) or as controversy (Fort Hood firing-squad execution livestream, Trump's wealth).

lanes.label: Pushback
lanes.description: Posts doubting, mocking, fact-checking or arguing against the dominant narratives.

posts.text:
ICYMI O/N

IRAN:

Trump said the Iran war was “essentially almost over” during his Nebraska speech, calling higher gasoline prices a “small price to pay” to prevent Tehran obtaining a nuclear weapon. (Iran International)  

Saudi and Yemeni forces launched an offensive to retake Mokha and ease the threat to shipping through Bab al-Mandeb, with around 100 fighters providing air cover, the Saudi-led coalition said. A Yemeni spokesman claimed control of the strait, which WSJ couldn’t independently confirm. (WSJ)    

The Houthis said they launched missile and drone attacks against Riyadh’s airport, Aramco’s Rabigh refinery and Saudi military installations in response to the offensive. Their spokesman warned airlines that Saudi airspace had become a theatre for their operations. (WSJ)  

Fars published footage claiming a fire at an Aramco facility in Jeddah following a Yemeni attack. The facility’s identity, damage and operational impact remain unconfirmed. (Fars)  

The U.S. withdrew 12 B-1 bombers from RAF Fairford over an IRGC-linked drone threat, U.S. and European officials told WSJ. Officials described a broader plot against aircraft and American pilots; British officials cautioned there was no evidence Tehran could execute an operation of that complexity. (WSJ)  

Gulf oil flows excluding Iran surged to over 81% of pre-war levels in September, data showed, led by a recovery in Saudi exports, while Iranian exports fell to zero due to a US blockade. (RTRS)

At least 50 tankers carrying Iranian oil remain backed up near Iran under the US blockade, according to United Against Nuclear Iran. Bloomberg’s preliminary tracking estimates show Iran loaded no crude onto tankers in September, the first zero-loading month since the war began. (BBG)  

Iranian Interior Minister Momeni said talks in Doha addressed Qatar and Pakistan’s mediation efforts, with proposals discussed aimed at reducing regional tensions and averting further war. (IRNA)

UN Secretary-General António Guterres arrived in Islamabad for a three-day visit, with Iran-US mediation among the subjects for talks with Pakistan’s political and military leadership. No breakthrough was announced. (IRNA)  

Recovering Hormuz crude flows aren’t resolving the diesel shortage: crude shipments reached 76% of prewar levels, but refined products accounted for just 11% of total oil flows versus over 20% before the war. Damaged refineries mean a full recovery could take well into 2027, analysts told WSJ. (WSJ)  

Trump signed an order allowing wider on-road use of tax-exempt red diesel, effectively offering a 24-cent-a-gallon federal tax saving. The IRS will waive penalties on highway sales through year-end; energy specialists warned limited distribution could constrain the benefit. (BBG)  

The World Bank warned that Asian governments’ energy subsidies may prove unsustainable, forecasting Middle East oil exports would not regain pre-war levels until mid-2027. It nevertheless raised its 2026 East Asia and Pacific growth forecast to 4.5%, citing AI investment and exports. (BBG)  

MACRO:

US borrowing costs for companies rated CCC or below reached 17%, the highest since May 2020, as the Treasury sell-off spreads into corporate credit. BofA cut its forecast for this month’s investment-grade issuance to $110bn from roughly $160bn. (FT)  

Commercial-property buyers are demanding price cuts or threatening to abandon deals as financing costs rise, WSJ reports. The share of CMBS mortgages in special servicing reached 11.42% in August, its highest since February 2013, according to Trepp. (WSJ) 

FT’s Unhedged column flags a potential dollar vulnerability: huge foreign inflows into US AI assets and falling currency hedging have left investors heavily exposed to USD. An AI reversal or renewed hedging could trigger substantial dollar selling, drawing on Nomura and BNY analysis. (FT)  

An OECD survey of 8,000 employers found just 1% of firms adopting AI were cutting headcount mainly because of the technology. FT reports economists remain sceptical of predictions of mass job losses, despite slowing entry-level tech hiring. (FT)  

HSBC maintains its call for further steepening in the U.S. 5s30s Treasury curve. Strategist Dhiraj Narula said volatility and the lack of clear technical resistance are keeping investors sidelined despite increasingly attractive long-end yields. (WSJ) 

The BoJ may signal this month that underlying inflation has roughly hit its 2% target, according to Reuters sources, highlighting its readiness to raise interest rates again in the coming months. Many in the central bank are cautious about delivering another hike this month. (RTRS)

BoJ Governor Ueda said on Tuesday it was becoming more important to anchor underlying inflation around the central bank's 2% target, signalling readiness to keep raising interest rates to blunt the risk of too-high inflation. (RTRS)

Japan’s 10-year auction was well received, where it attracted a bid-to-cover of 3.76, versus 3.29 previously and a 12-month average of 3.21; the tail narrowed to 0.02 from 0.12. JGB futures pared losses as yields above 3% brought buyers back. (BBG)  

Citi’s Tomohisa Fujiki said JGB yields are approaching their peaks, with 2.5–3% fair value for the 10-year if inflation stabilises near 2%. Citi expects curve flattening and warned crowded long-bank/short-property positioning could reverse. (BBG)  

US VP Vance told reporters that the $54bn Alaska LNG project with South Korea would proceed, despite Seoul making participation conditional on commercial viability and Trump threatening trade retaliation. South Korea said it transferred the first $2.4bn of investment funding under the US trade deal last week. (BBG)

SocGen remains neutral on Korean equities and prefers Taiwan as memory-chip earnings momentum fades and buyers disappear. Foreign investors sold $25bn of Korean stocks in August–September, while turnover has fallen around 75% from June’s peak; strategists described an “absence of marginal buyers.” (WSJ)    

South Korea’s President Lee said there were signs AI was used in attacks exposing customer data at seven financial firms. Hackers appear to have targeted third-party systems rather than core payment networks; no stolen funds have been reported. (FT)  

Australia’s Westpac consumer sentiment index fell 4.7% to 80.4 following the RBA hike and continued fuel-price pressure. Responses collected after the rate decision registered just 67.2; Westpac expects another hike in November. (BBG) 

Australian Treasurer Jim Chalmers told Bloomberg TV that higher bond yields would squeeze the budget as cheap debt is refinanced. He will incorporate the impact into the year-end budget update; RBC estimates current market yields could add about A$6bn to four-year costs. (BBG)   

New Zealand’s NZIER survey showed a net 43% of firms expecting economic improvement, with seasonally adjusted confidence the strongest since 2014. Actual demand remained weak, while fewer businesses planned price rises, suggesting limited pass-through of higher costs. (BBG) 

New Zealand’s governing National Party fell to 25.9%, its weakest polling result since 2020, in an RNZ-Reid Research survey ahead of November’s election. Neither main bloc would command a majority, leaving the centrist Opportunity Party potentially holding the balance of power. (BBG)   

Germany’s coalition is struggling to agree tax measures worth more than €4bn annually, with disputes over sugar, plastics and crypto gains threatening the budget deal. One official told Bloomberg that November approval of the 2027 budget could no longer be assumed. (BBG)  

German factory orders fell 10.6% M/M in August versus -1% expected, following July’s 3.2% rise. Large orders drove the decline: excluding them, orders slipped just 0.1%, while the three-month measure remained up 1.3%. (BBG)  

Germany’s AfD is expected to secure its first regional parliament presidency in Saxony-Anhalt on Tuesday with support from the hard-left BSW. The party is separately seeking enough votes to install its first state premier. (FT)  

French far-right presidential candidate Marine Le Pen presents plans on Tuesday to cut government spending by €25 billion ($28 billion) a year, seeking to establish her fiscal credibility in the face of a growing bond market crisis. (RTRS)

France’s 10-year borrowing costs have approached 5%, with its spread over Bunds widening by almost two-thirds in a month to around 140bp. FT reports growing investor concern that political resistance to budget cuts could turn the sell-off into a broader Eurozone crisis. (FT)  

France faces more than $1tn of debt maturities by 2030 and plans roughly $380bn of issuance next year, as traditional buyers retreat and borrowing costs approach 5%. WSJ reports debt-servicing costs are projected to rise 59% by 2030, with political paralysis undermining efforts to contain spending. (WSJ)  

French teachers are joining nationwide student protests demanding more education spending, adding pressure as the government seeks budget restraint. National Rally said it wants to avoid worsening the bond crisis and acknowledged that toppling the government could contribute to an escalation. (BBG)  

Czech inflation accelerated more than expected last month after the central bank warned that tighter monetary policy may be warranted to tame price growth. (BBG)

Philippine September CPI accelerated to 7.2% Y/Y versus 6.8% expected, ending four months of slowing inflation. Food and fuel drove the upside surprise, strengthening the case for further BSP tightening at its October 22 meeting. (BBG)

Thai September CPI rose 2.82% Y/Y versus 3.1% expected and 2.53% previously. The Commerce Ministry expects further acceleration in Q4 as fuel costs feed through, with flooding estimated to add around 0.1 percentage point to inflation. (BBG)  

EQUITIES:

OpenAI is discussing a $30bn funding round with UAE investors including MGX and with BlackRock, according to Bloomberg sources. The UAE syndicate could contribute up to $10bn; OpenAI is pitching a roughly $1.4tn pre-money valuation. (BBG)  

Wall Street banks have launched a record $60bn financing tied to Broadcom chips for Anthropic, according to the FT. (FT)  

Nvidia-backed Reflection launched its first open-weight model, Beam, targeting Chinese rivals in coding and agentic tasks. Reflection says it competes with https://t.co/da7jebtExB’s GLM-5.2 and is approaching Qwen3.8-Max; the model activates 23bn of its 501bn parameters per task. (RTRS)  

SemiAnalysis estimates Claude subscriptions offer roughly five times the API-equivalent value of comparable mid-tier ChatGPT plans following OpenAI’s limit reductions. Its analysis highlights subscription subsidies as a significant drag on AI-lab inference margins. (SemiAnalysis)  

Google is nearing a multiyear nuclear-power agreement worth at least $1bn with Constellation, according to Bloomberg sources. An announcement could come this week; the capacity and location have not been established. (BBG) 

AMD’s Lisa Su said demand still exceeds supply across CPUs, GPUs and AI products, and AMD will increase its previously announced $10bn Taiwan supply-chain investment. Supply should rise substantially in 2027, but customers could absorb more; planning now extends three to five years ahead. (China Times) 

OpenAI and Anthropic told Australian parliament on Tuesday they would welcome laws requiring them to report data breaches carried out by their AI agents, acknowledging the decision to notify authorities was currently at their discretion. (RTRS)

Oracle’s 2025 healthcare breach affected nearly 20 million people, according to newly reported disclosures from the Texas attorney general. The compromised information included Social Security numbers and medical records; the scale had not previously been disclosed. (BBG)   

Banks are expanding into Asian GPU lending, broadening funding for the AI buildout despite uncertainty over chip depreciation. Citi, JPMorgan, Barclays, Deutsche Bank, Santander and SMBC are evaluating GPU-linked loans, according to Bloomberg sources. (BBG)  

KKR’s retail private-credit fund K-FITS will exceed its 5% quarterly redemption cap to meet all requests, after withdrawals reached 5.06% of shares versus 3.43% previously. The fund cited sufficient liquidity to fulfil the requests in full. (BBG)  

DayOne Data Centers publicly filed for a US IPO after previously exploring a raise of up to $5bn at around $20bn valuation. Its filing showed first-half revenue rising to $512m from $151.5m, while its net loss widened to $81.9m. (BBG)  

NextEra’s $67bn Dominion takeover faces growing political opposition in Virginia, with Governor Abigail Spanberger seeking concessions on electricity bills, jobs and investment. FT reports the backlash is raising pressure for tougher approval conditions despite improved customer credits and employment guarantees. (FT)  

Korean memory suppliers are quoting sharply higher HBM4 long-term contract prices for 2027, according to DIGITIMES supply-chain reporting: approximately $1,400–1,600 versus $500–550 in 2026. (DIGITIMES)  

Seagate and Toshiba are competing for TDK’s hard-drive magnetic-heads business in a potential multibillion-dollar deal, Bloomberg sources said. TDK is the only independent supplier of the component; its shares jumped 7.3% as the bidders seek to secure AI storage supply. (BBG)  

DeepSeek is close to raising at least 80bn yuan ($12bn), exceeding its original 50bn-yuan target, according to Bloomberg sources. Tencent and CATL are among the largest backers, with signed term sheets potentially taking the round toward 100bn yuan ahead of an early-2027 IPO. (BBG)  

Moonshot AI completed its final private funding round at roughly $50bn valuation and is targeting a Hong Kong IPO in Q1 2027, according to Bloomberg sources. Early investor meetings could begin this month; the company has considered raising up to $5bn. (BBG)  

Grab and GoTo face mounting pressure from driver protests, high fuel costs and tighter commission rules across south-east Asia. Their long-running merger talks remain on hold because of Indonesian policy uncertainty, according to FT sources. (FT)  

CVC increased its Recordati offer to €53 per share from €51.29, valuing the pharmaceutical company at €10.5bn. The revised bid remains below the €60 sought by shareholder Palliser; Recordati closed Monday at €52.20. (BBG)  

BPCE acquired roughly 7% of Banco Sabadell, will receive board representation and committed to keeping its stake below 10%. The banks described the investment as friendly and will explore cooperation across investment banking, leasing and consumer credit. (BBG)

Donald Trump approved the first military execution in the US in more than 60 years

The president authorized the execution of former major and Army psychiatrist Nidal Hasan, who carried out a mass shooting at Fort Hood in Texas in 2009. The sentence is planned to be carried out by firing squad.

 The recommendation to Trump was submitted by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.

Hasan killed 13 people and wounded more than 30. After his arrest, he was left partially paralyzed and spent more than ten years in the military prison at Leavenworth.

For the US Army, this will be the first execution of a death sentence since 1961. Firing squads have not been used in the US military since the time of World War II.

El presidente Donald Trump aprobó la ejecución por pelotón de fusilamiento del exmayor del Ejército Nidal Malik Hasan, condenado a muerte por la masacre de Fort Hood (Texas) en 2009.
El 5 de octubre de 2026, el portavoz del Pentágono, Sean Parnell, anunció en X que el secretario de Guerra, Pete Hegseth, recomendó la pena y que Trump la autorizó. El secretario del Ejército fijará la fecha y el lugar. Hegseth respondió al anuncio con la palabra “Justicia”.
Hasan, entonces psiquiatra militar con rango de mayor, abrió fuego el 5 de noviembre de 2009 en un centro de procesamiento de personal de Fort Hood contra soldados en su mayoría desarmados. Mató a 13 personas (12 militares en activo y un retirado) e hirió a otras 32, mientras gritaba “Allahu Akbar”. El ataque se vinculó a su radicalización y a contactos previos con un clérigo de Al Qaeda; él lo describió después como represalia por las guerras de EE.UU. en países musulmanes. Quedó parapléjico por las heridas que recibió al ser reducido.
En 2013 un tribunal militar lo condenó por 13 cargos de asesinato premeditado y 32 de intento de asesinato premeditado, y recomendó por unanimidad la pena de muerte. Desde entonces permanece en la prisión militar de Fort Leavenworth (Kansas).
Según el Código Uniforme de Justicia Militar, una sentencia de muerte impuesta por consejo de guerra no puede ejecutarse sin la aprobación del presidente. Si se lleva a cabo, sería la primera ejecución militar en EE.UU. desde 1961 (cuando se ahorcó al soldado John Bennett) y la primera por fusilamiento del Ejército desde la Segunda Guerra Mundial (1945). La aprobación inicia trámites, pero Hasan podría retrasarlos años con recursos de hábeas corpus en la justicia civil federal.

Delivering Justice: Trump Cuts Through Years of Paralysis to Order Firing Squad Execution for Fort Hood Terrorist

For more than a decade, the families of the 13 Americans murdered at Fort Hood in 2009 were forced to endure an agonizing wait, watching justice stalled by bureaucratic inertia and a political establishment hesitant to enforce the law. That era of hesitation came to an abrupt end when President Donald Trump, acting on a recommendation from Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, officially signed off on the execution of convicted mass murderer Nidal Hasan by military firing squad.

The decisive action marks the first military execution approved in over six decades, sending a clear, uncompromising message: those who wage war against the United States Armed Forces on American soil will face the ultimate consequence under military law.

Overcoming Years of Bureaucratic Stalling
In November 2009, Hasan opened fire on unarmed soldiers at a readiness center in Fort Hood, Texas, killing 12 active-duty service members and a retired soldier, while wounding more than 30 others. Hasan openly pledged allegiance to enemy fighters and admitted in court that his massacre was an act of war against U.S. service members.

A military jury unanimously convicted Hasan in 2013 and sentenced him to death. Yet despite the clear, indisputable verdict and the sheer magnitude of the atrocity, successive administrations allowed the killer to languish comfortably on death row at Fort Leavenworth, Kansas. For years, progressive legal groups and left-wing activists worked tirelessly to drag out the appeals process, shielding a self-confessed terrorist from paying the price prescribed by military justice.

Where others wavered, President Trump demonstrated the resolve expected of a Commander-in-Chief. By approving the firing squad—a method reinstated to bypass logistical hurdles and drug shortages engineered by activist groups—the administration cut through years of procedural gridlock to finally enforce the jury's lawful sentence.

The decision highlights a stark divide in American politics. While the Trump administration moved swiftly to stand with gold star families, military personnel, and victims of terror, left-wing critics immediately rushed to condemn the decision, expressing more outrage over the method of execution than the cold-blooded murder of 13 patriots.

For years, progressive policies and legal advocacy have prioritized the comforts and legal technicalities of violent offenders over the moral obligation owed to victims and their survivors. While liberal commentators decried the return to traditional military justice, veterans’ organizations and families of the fallen celebrated the move as an essential restoration of accountability, deterrence, and honor within the ranks.

The Secretary of the Army will designate the date and location for the sentence to be carried out. For the survivors and families who carried the burden of Hasan’s attack for over 15 years, the decision represents more than a legal conclusion—it represents a Commander-in-Chief willing to back the military, uphold the rule of law, and deliver long-overdue justice without apology.

posts.text:
Networks Giddily Promote Bad Polls, Seek to Depress GOP Turnout Ahead of Midterms | Curtis Houck, Newsbusters

Whereas the broadcast networks spent the days prior to the 2022 midterms ensconced in January 6 Committee hearings, talk of the 2020 election, and demands that no one assign blame for the bad economy, the elitist networks of ABC, CBS, and NBC continued on Monday morning to emphasize the impending blue tsunami through negative polls, treating President Trump seeking to drive base turnout as a five-alarm fire, and largely ignoring Democratic opposition.

ABC’s Good Morning America had the shortest segment by far, but they certainly didn’t skimp on the doomcasting.

Co-host and former Clinton official George Stephanopoulos sounded like the true partisan tool that he is: “With midterms less than a month away and his poll numbers at record lows, the President is hitting the trail in deep-red states to shore up Republicans facing strong headwinds.”

Chief White House correspondent Mary Bruce also did her part for her preferred political party by seeking to depress GOP turnout, painting a seemingly insurmountable picture:

[A]s we head into this final sprint, President Trump is ramping up his campaign appearances in red states that he won, playing defense for the GOP on their home turf. This morning, with less than a month until the midterms, President Trump is hitting the campaign trail in deep-red states, hoping to boost turnout with his base.

Bruce hit all the correct notes for her handlers at the Democratic National Committee headquarters, including the high gas prices. She at least, thought, mentioned out loud the name of a Democrat who isn’t James Talarico:

BRUCE: Today, he heads to Nebraska, a state he won by 20 points to campaign for incumbent Senator Pete Ricketts, as he faces union leader Dan Osborne, an independent who’s backed by Democrats. And, on Wednesday, Trump’s back in Texas, his second stop in the span of a week to bolster Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, who’s trailing in the polls behind Democrat James Talarico. Trump has been blitzing traditional Republican strongholds. In the past week, visiting Texas, Oklahoma, Alabama, and Ohio, all states he won by double digits, but that could now determine control of Congress.

TRUMP: Nobody counted on the fact that Trump was going to go out and campaign for all these people.

BRUCE: The President is urging voters to act like he’s on the ballot. But it comes as he’s facing record-low approval numbers, and with Americans feeling the economic fallout from the war with Iran: at the pump, gas now averaging $4.30 a gallon, diesel at $6.30.

“IOWA FARMER” DAN PEDERSON: You just cannot keep these high-priced fuel going for another six to nine months. It — just — it’s unsustainable. It’s just crazy.

After having arrived much later at the daily midterm beat (compared to ABC and CBS), NBC’s Today led both hours with the push to November.

Co-host Savannah Guthrie boasted in a tease the latest poll numbers are a “red alert,” with “Trump traveling to reliable Republican strongholds four weeks from election day as our new NBC News poll shows the party on shaky ground even in the rubiest red states.”

“High-profile Republicans sounding the alarm...as these Trump ads, paid for by taxpayers, get prime airtime during some football. We’re live in Washington straight ahead,” she added.

There again, the elitist press go with their misleading narrative that a Republican president traveling to red states ahead of an election is a definitive, no-doubt-about-it sign of a blue wave. In doing so, they’re purposefully ignoring the basic political need to turn out one’s base.

Senior White House correspondent Gabe Gutierrez had the story, starting with that misleading framing: “The President is spending a lot of time in traditionally red states defending areas that usually aren’t all that competitive at the polls. White House officials often say he is his own best messenger.”

“The President in Ohio this weekend, one of four usually reliable Republican states where he has rallied his base over the past week. Today he heads to Nebraska, a state won by 20 points in 2024, but where a GOP incumbent is now trying to hold on to his Senate seat,” he added.

Gutierrez mixed in Trump promises of “$90 rebate checks to seniors on Medicare” and a $5,000 dividend to every American if the GOP wins next month, with declarations that “Democrats see an opening” on cost of living because “[e]ven some Republicans are worried soaring gas and grocery prices could still trouble this election.”

Before wrapping the first hour with two notes on new GOP ads (one from the White House, another from a Texas super PAC), Gutierrez hawked a new, negative poll for Trump: “A new NBC News/Telemundo poll finds Democrats now lead Republicans by 24 points among critical Latino voters on which party they want controlling Congress. The President’s approval rating among Latinos? Just 27 percent.”

CBS Mornings had two full segments in its first hour, packed the brim with zero cause for concern by Democrats as it was encroaching on do-no-wrong territory.

Featured co-host Vladimir Duthiers stacked the deck by touting “new signs of trouble for Republicans,” with CBS predicting Democrats will romp to a 23-seat margin of victory in the House because “[v]oters do not approve of President Trump’s handling of the economy and inflation.”

Stating it as though it’s bizarre for him to even try, Duthiers added Trump is “still campaigning hard, though, hoping to turn the tide.”

Chief White House correspondent Nancy Cordes similarly scoffed, “Another day, another red-state campaign stop planned for President Trump. This time, he’s heading to Nebraska, which he won by 20 points two years ago, but where the Senate race today is a little too close for comfort.”

Cordes continued:

TRUMP: They are a bunch of dumb son of a [EXPLETIVE].

CORDES: President Trump deploying some coarse language to describe Democrats this weekend as the outlook for his party gets muddier. A New York Times poll shows Democratic candidates for governor pulling ahead of the Republican rivals in four red states.

TRUMP: Just get out and vote. If you do that, we’re going to win, and we’re going to win big.

CORDES: Trump was stumping for Ohio Senator John Husted, who’s fending off a challenge from Sherrod Brown, who is hoping to reclaim the seat he lost two years ago.

FORMER SENATOR SHERROD BROWN (D-OH): We’ve got to address high costs. More money going out the door than coming in. I hope the President changes his focus and realizes how important that is.

CORDES: The Democratic inroads are forcing Republicans to make some tough choices. Over the weekend, the top GOP super PAC stopped airing ads in swing-state North Carolina, shifting those funds to Kansas instead. Ahead of the election, Trump is trying to appeal voters’ bank accounts, announcing plans to send some seniors on Medicare $90 to help with premium costs, and repeating his vow to give Americans cash if Republicans win.

TRUMP: I’m going to give all adult citizens in the United States of America $5,000.

CORDES: It’s an unusual campaign promise that other Republicans are shying away from. Arizona Democrat Mark Kelly called it corrupt.

SENATOR MARK KELLY (D-AZ) [on CBS’s Face the Nation, 10/04/26]: I mean, this is just a payoff and he’s trying to buy votes.

A new Texas Southern University poll of Fort Bend County has James Talarico up 18 over Ken Paxton, 56 to 38. Before anyone panics or celebrates, some context.

☠️ The U.S. military is preparing to use a firing squad for the first time in generations.

Nidal Hasan is now scheduled to be executed by U.S. Army firing squad on December 3, 2026, at 1 p.m. Central at Fort Hood, Texas. President Trump approved the firing-squad method after a recommendation from Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, and the Army subsequently set the date. 

Hasan was the Army psychiatrist convicted of the November 5, 2009 Fort Hood mass shooting, where he killed 13 people and wounded 32. He was sentenced to death by court-martial in 2013. 

What makes this such a huge story is the precedent: if carried out, it would be the first U.S. military execution since 1961 and the first military firing-squad execution since World War II. 

There’s also an important distinction from ordinary state executions. This isn’t Texas carrying out a Texas death sentence. It’s a military execution under the Uniform Code of Military Justice, and military death sentences require presidential approval before they can be carried out. 

Hasan is also paralyzed from the waist down after being shot by police during the 2009 attack, which raises a very practical question about how the Army will physically position and secure him for a firing squad. Public reporting so far confirms the method, date and location, but I have not yet seen a publicly released Army protocol describing the exact firing-squad setup for Hasan. 

And it still may not happen exactly as scheduled. Although his military appeals have run their course, reporting notes that he could still pursue federal habeas corpus litigation, which could potentially delay the execution. ☠️

posts.text:
Lower Taxes, Safer Streets, Stronger Border: President Trump’s Texas Record

FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE

Today, President Donald J. Trump returns to Texas with a record of results: historic tax relief, the most secure border in a generation, safer streets, and a surge of new private investment creating jobs across the Lone Star State.

Tax Relief for Texas Workers, Families, Seniors

President Trump’s Working Families Tax Cuts is putting money back in Texans’ pockets.
• No Tax on Overtime: Approximately one in four Texas workers no longer pay federal income taxes on qualifying overtime pay.
• No Tax on Social Security: About four million Texas seniors benefit from the new senior deduction.
• Bigger Refunds: Texas taxpayers saw average refunds of $4,344 the second-highest in the nation.
• Rural Health Investments: Texas secured about $281 million in first-year Rural Health Transformation Program funding.
• Protecting Jobs and Wages: The Working Families Tax Cuts safeguarded 547,000 Texas jobs, $107 billion in state GDP, and $51 billion in workers’ wages.

Safer Streets Across Texas

Violent crime is falling across the state as a result of President Trump’s law-and-order agenda.
• Violent crime fell 13% last year, including a 13% drop in murder and 11% drop in rape.
• The top 25 most populous jurisdictions in Texas all posted lower overall crime rates than the year before.
• In the first half of 2026, Arlington homicides fell 60% from the first half of 2025.
• America’s Safest Big Cities recently placed Plano, Laredo, and Arlington in the national Top 20 with Plano and Laredo in the Top 10.

The Most Secure Border in a Generation

President Trump ended the Biden-era border crisis and is reimbursing Texas for the costs it carried.
• The Trump Administration has not released a single illegal alien at the border for 16 straight months.
• Southern border apprehensions in August were 94% lower than the monthly average under Biden.
• Refugee admissions in the first ten months of this fiscal year are down almost 90% from 2024.
• The Working Families Tax Cuts $46.5 billion to finish the border wall.
• Texas will soon receive $7.5 billion from the State Border Security Reinforcement Fund established in the Working Families Tax Cuts to recover costs from Biden’s border crisis.

Protecting Texas Communities

President Trump is delivering for Texas farmers, ranchers, and everyday families.
• Water for the Valley: In January 2026, USDA and the State Department secured Mexico’s commitment to deliver 350,000 acre-feet per year from the Rio Grande meeting the 1944 treaty average and repaying prior-cycle debt.
• Protecting Ratepayers: After President Trump’s landmark Ratepayer Protection Pledge, the Public Utility Commission of Texas and ERCOT have moved to shield Texas families from the cost of data center expansion.
• Screwworm Response: The Trump Administration funded additional Texas Animal Health Commission inspectors and a new $750 million sterile-fly facility, which broke ground in April at Moore Air Base in Edinburg.
• Support for Farmers: The Trump Administration has delivered $827 million to more than 33,000 Texas farmers through the Emergency Commodity Assistance Program for the 2024 crop year. Nearly 27,000 Texas producers have also received more than $832 million in Farmer Bridge Assistance payments as part of a $12 billion national bridge program for trade disruptions and higher input costs left by the Biden Administration.

A Private Investment Boom in Texas

President Trump’s agenda of tax cuts, energy dominance, secure borders, and pro-growth policies has drawn major capital to the Lone Star State.
• Bristol Myers Squibb announced a $2.3 billion investment to build a new multi-modal manufacturing campus in Houston.
• Toyo Co. announced a $357 million investment to build a solar cell manufacturing facility near Houston, creating 400 American jobs.
• Toyota announced a $3.6 billion investment at its San Antonio campus to build the new Tacoma in the United States instead of Mexico, creating 2,000 American jobs.
• Saronic announced it will build a new $3.2 billion shipyard in Brownsville.
• Micron announced $500 million in strategic financing to advance development and manufacturing at its Sherman facility.
• FormFactor announced a $140 million investment for a new probe card manufacturing facility in Farmers Branch, creating more than 600 American jobs.
• In July, ZERLUMA broke ground on a $50 million aluminum recycling and advanced manufacturing facility in Mission.
• SpaceX announced a $16.8 billion investment for the first phase of its new semiconductor fabrication plant in Grimes County.
• USG Corporation announced a $1.18 billion investment to build a new production facility in Orange, creating 200 American jobs.
• Grupo Bimbo announced a $1 billion investment affirming its commitment to the U.S. market.
• XPEL announced a $60 million investment to expand manufacturing and operations in San Antonio.
• Tesla announced a $3 billion investment in a research chip facility at its Giga Texas campus.
• Avant Technology announced a $20 million investment to expand its manufacturing facility in Pharr, creating 250 American jobs.
• America First Refining and Reliance announced a multi-billion-dollar energy partnership to open the first new U.S. oil refinery in nearly half a century in Brownsville.
• MP Materials announced a more than $1.25 billion investment in a new large-scale rare-earth magnet manufacturing campus in Northlake, creating more than 1,500 direct manufacturing and engineering jobs.
• Arm Inc. announced a $71 million investment to expand its Austin campus with a new semiconductor lab, creating more than 320 American jobs.
• Vantage Data Centers announced a $25 billion investment to build a 1,200-acre data center campus in Shackelford County.
• Inventec announced an $85 million investment to build a manufacturing base in Texas to support AI server shipments.
• Wistron announced a $500 million investment to acquire land and facilities in Dallas for high-performance computing devices.
• LGM Pharma announced a $6 million investment to expand its Rosenberg manufacturing facility.
• Paris Baguette announced a $160 million investment to build the company’s first North American production site, creating 450 American jobs.

President Trump and Republicans are proving once again that America First means Texas First lower taxes, a sealed border, safer communities, and jobs that stay in the United States. Texans have a choice: continue that progress, or let Democrats tear it all down.

Distributed on October 7th, 2026.

🚨 TRUMP REDET VON RAKETEN AUF LOS ANGELES!!

Ich habe die Zahl zweimal nachgeschlagen. Die 30-jährige US-Staatsanleihe stand gestern zeitweise bei 5,71 Prozent, so hoch wie seit 2002 nicht mehr. Ein paar Stunden später steht der US-Präsident auf einer Wahlkampfbühne in Texas und sagt: "Lasst sie San Diego treffen."

#Bitcoin hängt mit 82.781 Dollar am unteren Rand seiner Spanne, und aus den Bitcoin-ETFs sind an einem einzigen Tag 484,9 Millionen Dollar abgeflossen.

Erst die letzten 24 Stunden im Schnelldurchlauf, dann wer den "kleinen Preis" bezahlt, von dem Trump redet, und danach die eine Anleihe-Zahl, gegen die Bitcoin gerade verliert 👇

DIE NACHT IM SCHNELLDURCHLAUF

→ 🟡 Die zehnjährige US-Rendite steigt zeitweise auf 5,35 Prozent, höchster Stand seit 2002. Am 22. September stand sie noch bei 4,96 Prozent

→ 🟡 Danach die Auktion: 39 Milliarden Dollar Zehnjährige gehen zu 5,300 Prozent weg, bei 2,77-facher Nachfrage. Die indirekten Bieter, darunter ausländische Notenbanken, nehmen 80,3 Prozent, die Händlerbanken nur 2,5. Käufer gibt es also, zu 5,3 Prozent

→ 🏛️ Eine Stunde später das Fed-Protokoll: Die Erhöhung im September auf 3,75 bis 4,00 Prozent war die erste seit 2023, die meisten Notenbanker halten eine weitere bis Jahresende für angemessen. Den Anstieg am langen Ende erklärt die Fed vor allem mit höheren Realzinsen

→ 🟡 In London ist es noch heftiger. Die 30-jährige britische Staatsanleihe erreicht 6,04 Prozent, höchster Stand seit Januar 1998. Laut Financial Times hat der Iran-Krieg Londons Haushaltspuffer von 23,6 auf etwa 12 Milliarden Pfund halbiert, rund 10 Milliarden davon fressen höhere Zinsen

→ 🟡 Frankreich zahlt für zehn Jahre 4,83 Prozent, Deutschland knapp 3,5. Der Abstand wächst an einem Tag um 7 auf 134 Basispunkte. Nur Japan bleibt mit 3,11 Prozent ruhig

→ 🟡 Der 30-jährige US-Hypothekenzins springt um 19 Basispunkte auf 7,49 Prozent, höchster Stand seit November 2023. Die Kreditanträge fallen in einer Woche um 4,2 Prozent

→ ⚪ Laut Axios soll das Pentagon die Vorbereitungen für eine mögliche Wiederaufnahme großer Kampfhandlungen gegen den Iran abschließen, womöglich noch vor den Zwischenwahlen. Brent steht über 101 Dollar. Meine öffentliche Wette, dass vor dem 3. November keine US-Bombe iranischen Boden trifft, steht damit auf dem Prüfstand

→ ⚪ US-Außenminister Marco Rubio sagt, der Iran habe die Kontrolle über die Straße von Hormus verloren, es fließe so viel Öl wie vor dem Konflikt. Finanzminister Scott Bessent ergänzt, der Iran habe seit dem 25. August kein Fass mehr verladen. Der Ölpreis über 100 Dollar glaubt beiden noch nicht

→ 📉 Die Wall Street gibt nach: Dow minus 0,66 Prozent auf 51.180 Punkte, S&P 500 und Nasdaq je 0,2 Prozent unter ihren Rekorden. Am Dienstag hatte der S&P zum ersten Mal über 7.800 geschlossen

→ 🟡 Gold verliert im Tagesverlauf rund zwei Prozent und testet die 4.100 Dollar. Steigende Realzinsen treffen auch das älteste sichere Geld

→ 🤖 Samsung erwartet für das dritte Quartal 107,4 Billionen Won Betriebsgewinn, rund 80 Milliarden Dollar, nach 12,2 Billionen vor einem Jahr. KI-Firmen kaufen die Speicherchips leer, die DRAM-Vertragspreise sollen im vierten Quartal um 10 bis 15 Prozent steigen

→ 🟠 Bei den Bitcoin-ETFs ist es der größte Tagesabfluss seit dem 25. Juni, allein BlackRocks IBIT verliert 207,7 Millionen. Auf der anderen Seite nimmt Robinhood 25 Millionen Dollar Bitcoin in die eigene Bilanz

→ 💥 Über alle Coins werden in 24 Stunden 342 Millionen Dollar an Long-Positionen liquidiert, gegen 54 Millionen Shorts. $ETH steht bei 2.571 Dollar, $SOL bei 115,43, $XRP fällt um 3,9 Prozent auf 1,41

⭐ "LASST SIE SAN DIEGO TREFFEN"

Am Montag in Nebraska fiel der Satz zum ersten Mal. Trump nannte die hohen Spritpreise im Krieg "künstlich" und "einen kleinen Preis", dann: "Lasst sie Los Angeles ausschalten, lasst sie San Diego ausschalten." In der Nacht auf heute legte er in San Antonio nach: "Wollt ihr eine Horrorshow sehen? Lasst sie San Diego treffen. Lasst sie Los Angeles treffen." Danach versicherte er, die Regierung schütze ihre Städte.

Steven Cheung, Kommunikationschef des Weißen Hauses, sagt, gemeint sei: Ein Iran mit Atomwaffe hätte diese Städte bedroht. Kaliforniens Gouverneur Gavin Newsom fordert den 25. Verfassungszusatz, San Diegos Bürgermeister Todd Gloria sagt, seine Stadt sei "kein Kollateralschaden".

🟠 BITCOIN GEGEN 2,91 PROZENT ÜBER DER INFLATION

Die wichtigste Zahl für Bitcoin steht gerade in keinem Krypto-Chart. Die zehnjährige inflationsgeschützte US-Anleihe bringt 2,91 Prozent Rendite über der Teuerung. Am 6. Oktober 2025, dem Tag des Allzeithochs bei 126.080 Dollar, waren es 1,84 Prozent. Seitdem ist dieser Realzins um gut einen Prozentpunkt gestiegen, und Bitcoin steht 34 Prozent tiefer.

Ein Staat, der dir fast drei Prozent über der Inflation garantiert, ist der härteste Gegner, den Bitcoin haben kann. Die ETF-Anleger haben gestern gewählt, an genau dem Tag, an dem die Zehnjährige ihr Hoch seit 2002 machte.

Der Futures-Markt hält sich raus. Das Open Interest liegt bei 54,1 Milliarden Dollar, 1,2 Prozent weniger als vor 24 Stunden, das Funding bei Binance praktisch bei null. Der Fear and Greed Index fällt in zwei Tagen von 74 auf 63.

Worauf ich heute achte: Das Tief der letzten 24 Stunden liegt bei 82.664 Dollar, das Hoch bei 84.340. Ein Tagesschluss unter dem Tief macht die 80.000 zum nächsten Halt, oben muss Bitcoin erst die 84.340 zurückholen. Meine Kaufmarke bleibt 74.000. Ausbrüche mit Hebel kaufe ich nicht, solange der Realzins über 2,9 Prozent steht. Mein Signal für mehr Risiko wäre die Zehnjährige zurück unter 5,20 Prozent, und darauf habe ich öffentlich nicht gesetzt: Meine Wette sagt Schluss über 5,20 am Freitag.

🇩🇪 DEUTSCHLAND ZAHLT DEN ZINS ZWEIMAL

Die Bundesanleihe wirkt mit knapp 3,5 Prozent harmlos neben Washington und London. Für dich ist sie es nicht.

Erstens beim Kredit. Zehnjährige Bauzinsen lagen im September im Schnitt bei 4,11 Prozent, Anfang Oktober bei 4,44. Du finanzierst 400.000 Euro? Dann zahlst du rund 1.320 Euro mehr Zinsen im Jahr, für dasselbe Haus, weil Öl über 100 Dollar die Renditen weltweit nach oben zieht.

Zweitens über den Haushalt. Der Bund plant für 2027 Zinsausgaben von 41,9 Milliarden Euro, nach 30,3 Milliarden in diesem Jahr, und bis 2030 von 80,7 Milliarden. Damit überweist Finanzminister Lars Klingbeil schon 2027 mehr an die Gläubiger, als das ganze Verkehrsministerium mit 26,4 Milliarden ausgeben darf. Der Entwurf stammt aus dem Sommer, abgestimmt wird Ende November.

Wer in Deutschland einen Kredit hat und Steuern zahlt, trägt den Zinsanstieg doppelt, bei der Bank und über den Steuerbescheid.

Heute um 14:30 Uhr kommen in den USA die Erstanträge auf Arbeitslosenhilfe, um 19 Uhr versteigert das US-Finanzministerium rund 22 Milliarden Dollar an 30-jährigen Anleihen. Nach 5,71 Prozent am Mittwoch zeigt diese Auktion, ob die starke Nachfrage von gestern nur am Preis hing.

War der Anleihe-Teil heute zu viel oder genau richtig? Schreib es drunter. Danach entscheide ich, ob Staatsanleihen hier einen festen Block bekommen.

Keine Finanzielle Anlageberatung!

NYT: Trump’s midterm problem isn’t defectors. It’s Republicans who stay home.

“President Trump has been saying, ‘Vote as if I was on the ballot,’ and that’s exactly what I’m going to do — not vote,” said Brandon Tremaine, 24, a graduate student in Texas who voted for Mr. Trump in 2020. “You do not campaign on being the ticket of peace and start a war of choice that is directly hurting Americans here at home and gotten Americans killed overseas.”

Signs are emerging that dispirited Republican voters may stay home in November, bringing a Democratic surge without many conversions. Charlie Cook calls it the red undertow: not a rising Democratic tide, a drowning Trump brand.

My objection to James Talarico is not simply that he is a Democrat. It is that he wraps his political ideology in Christianity while publicly teaching things that directly contradict Scripture.

Talarico claims Christianity while using the Bible to advance political positions that I believe are fundamentally contrary to its teaching. That is precisely why I call him a wolf in sheep’s clothing. His profession of faith does not place his teachings beyond biblical scrutiny.

posts.name: Jan
posts.text:
Wednesday night at Freeman Coliseum was the first time a president has come back to San Antonio for a rally since 2019. Texans showed up for it.

Doors were set for late afternoon, and people were already in line hours before the program. Inside, the floor and the lower bowl were packed with red hats and flags, phones up, the usual Texas mix of families, veterans, and folks who drove in from outside Bexar County. Outside, more people stood behind the barricades by the tents and the screens so they could still watch. Freeman holds roughly 11,700 for a political setup, and security always eats some of that. 

Trump was there to boost Ken Paxton in the Senate race against James Talarico and Carlos De La Cruz in the redrawn 35th. 

Midterms do not usually fill a coliseum like this. Last night they did, because a lot of Texans still want to show up in person instead of just arguing online.

Proud of the turnout. Proud of the neighbors who made the trip!🇺🇸
#SanAntonio #Texas 
#FreemanColiseum

President Trump Is Putting American Industry, Jobs, and Paychecks Back on the Map

FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE

President Donald J. Trump is delivering on his promise to the American worker: build it here, power it here, and put paychecks back in the communities Washington left behind. In a matter of weeks, President Trump has locked in a run of steel, nuclear, gas, shipbuilding, and medical manufacturing commitments that will hire American workers and strengthen American security.
• President Trump announced that Mesabi Metallics will build a $15 billion steel complex in Iowa the largest steel plant ever built in the United States. Fed by American iron ore and driven by the Trump Administration’s steel tariffs, the fully integrated mine-to-mill complex will create 1,750 new, permanent jobs, support up to 6,000 construction jobs, and generate an estimated $95 billion in economic output.

• President Trump and Anduril announced Arsenal-2, the biggest new American shipyard push since World War II, now moving forward in Maryland. The yard will produce critical Virginia-class components and large assemblies, create about 3,100 direct jobs, and support more than 11,000 indirect jobs. Anduril is investing $3.7 billion in private capital; the Navy is putting up to $2.9 billion behind it as part of the Trump Administration’s push to reshore America’s defense industrial base.

• President Trump unveiled a South Korean energy investment package of up to $200 billion in the United States. The package includes as much as $120 billion to build eight large-scale nuclear plants, $54 billion tied to the Alaska LNG pipeline, and $22.3 billion for a six-gigawatt natural gas power facility in Texas.

• Vice President Vance announced that the Department of Energy will invest $150 million to advance a major new transmission line in Alaska. The project includes 223 miles linking the Beluga power station on the southern coast with Healy in the Interior, a corridor serving ports and nearly three-quarters of the state’s population.

• Becton Dickinson announced a $19 billion U.S. investment under a landmark partnership with the Trump Administration, including $3 billion to expand American manufacturing. BD will produce 100% of the needles it sells in America with American-made steel and expand domestic output of essential products.

• AstraZeneca announced a $1 billion investment in Massachusetts under the $50 billion investment commitment it made in its Most Favored Nation agreement with the Trump Administration. The company is expanding its domestic research and manufacturing operation and growing its domestic workforce.

October 8th, 2026.

posts.name: Paul A. Szypula 🇺🇸
posts.text:
James Talarico wants a Senate seat and hasn’t shown his face in almost two weeks. That’s a fair thing to ask about. His spokesperson saying he has the flu isn’t the same as the nominee showing up, or at least releasing a video.

Talarico’s last documented public event was a Robert De Niro fundraiser in New York on September 28. Ken Paxton says he was last seen in Texas on September 26. Thursday his campaign said he came down with the flu after more than 100 events and will be back this weekend. He hasn’t been on a trail in Texas.

His account has been posting, and it answered Trump on a debate. Nothing shows Talarico is the one typing those posts. A staffer can hit send.

Trump called him missing in action on Wednesday and said bad rumors were coming out. Paxton asked for proof of life today. The rumor part isn’t a story. Talarico’s absence is. Early voting in Texas starts October 19. A nominee who wants the job doesn’t get to spend the run-up to that as a statement from a staffer.

The flu can be real. Plenty of candidates get sick. The test is whether he comes back this weekend, in Texas, where the voters are. A post from bed doesn’t count. A fundraiser in New York two weeks ago doesn’t count either.

He needs to release a video and explain himself. If he can’t do that before early voting, he should drop out.

Paxton is using Talarico’s absence because it’s usable. Talarico handed him the opening. If his account can post, he can face a camera. Talarico expecting votes while he won’t show his face is unacceptable.

I refuse to listen to liberals lamenting a firing squad for the Fort Hood shooter, because a large share of the same voices glorified the killing of Charlie Kirk on video. A line now making the rounds says the price of this execution is your peace, your decency, and the soul of our society, and that we do not have to be this fake tough but real ugly way. On November 5, 2009, Army Major Nidal Malik Hasan opened fire in a processing center at Fort Hood, Texas, killed 13 people, wounded 32 others, and later called the attack jihad. A court-martial panel found him guilty in 2013 and sentenced him to death. President Trump approved that sentence on October 2, 2026, and the Army set a firing squad for December 3 at Fort Hood. That is the event now being dressed up as a threat to the national soul.

Charlie Kirk, founder of Turning Point USA, had not even committed a crime. On September 10, 2025, he was speaking and taking questions before about 3,000 people at Utah Valley University when Tyler Robinson, according to prosecutors, fired from a rooftop and killed him. No indictment was pending and no warrant had been issued, because there was no offense to answer. Video of the killing circulated at once, and a share of the commentary did not grieve it. It glorified it. Peace was not the word on those clips. Decency was not the posture. The soul of society, if that phrase means anything, was the thing being spent for applause. The same voices now want solemn language about a convicted mass murderer, as if the earlier celebration had not already spent the currency they are trying to invoice. I am not buying it.

posts.text:
President Trump comments on the planned execution of Nidal Hasan, the Fort Hood shooter, and the Pentagon’s proposal to livestream the firing squad.Hasan, a former Army psychiatrist, carried out the November 5, 2009, attack at Fort Hood, Texas, walking into a Soldier Readiness Processing Center, shouting “Allahu Akbar,” and opening fire on unarmed service members. The rampage killed 13 people and wounded more than 30 others. A military jury convicted him and sentenced him to death in 2013. 

After years of appeals, President Trump recently approved Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s recommendation that the sentence be carried out by Army firing squad, the first military execution since 1961 and the first by firing squad since World War II. It is currently scheduled for December 3, 2026, at Fort Hood. 

In remarks addressing the additional decision to make the execution public via livestream, Trump said he was not involved in that specific call but understood the rationale of setting an example. My analysis on the previous two weeks in Texas:

I don't want this guy to win. However, this is what 5D Chess actually looks like.

They probably had certain people from their campaign or media people to feed some individual "fake rumors" of Talarico's disappearance.

However, because they knew that some bimbos who are desperate for good news regarding this race would fall for it instead of focusing on how the Republicans can convince voters to show up by ending the Iran War, which would improve the economy, gas prices, grocery prices, which would then restore some credibility back, diffusing the Democrats' affordability argument, they then decided to believe the garbage stuff fed to them by Talarico's folks to make everyone on X go crazy and be distracted that Talarico was running millions of dollars in ADs and restrategizing the entire time (just like Trump did in 2024 by the way, he took like a 1-2 weeks off the campaign trail in the final month or two)...

...so that they could get Paxton to come out and egg on Talarico, only for Talarico to pull a 180 on everyone and now is doing the good 'ol "UNO REVERSE" card on Paxton because he knows Paxton doesn't want to debate him.

That's the 5D Chess that happened here and everyone fell for it. That's why I didn't say "MUH-TALARICO WAS IN A MENTAL HEALTH FACILITY" immediately. Trust me, I am a big conspiracy theorist, a big one. However, I analyzed the situation and inferred that this was a ploy to make Paxton look bad for not debating and because Talarico is up 2-3 points, he can afford 2-3 weeks off with ADs and door knockers running around the entire state.

It's called being objective and not a shill for a political party, even if that's your preference.

If something comes out about Talarico, then I'll apologize. But, as of right now:

It was a big nothing burger.

October 2026 Midterm Update:
(House, Senate, Governors)

Well here we are in October, things are about more or less the same aside from a few things, there are 5 states I want to focus on this time in order being, Alaska, Michigan, Ohio, Georgia and Kansas. (Also if your wondering why the Dems now have 228 seats in the House thank the Colorado GOP and Victor Marx)

To start things off with Alaska, you may have noticed the massive delta between the Senate and Governor races, this is because while the scandal has improved Sullivan's margin slightly, Alaska's stupid election system has resulted in 3 R's running on the same ballot for governor against one Dem, barring a miracle this race is over.   

Next up is Michigan and this one hurts to change as I've gone big on Rogers since the beginning of this cycle however it's clear at that this point that despite Sayed's connection to Piker and his 9/11 comments it's not going to determine the race for many indies which has essentially been Rogers entire campaign. 

Sayed has also mostly united the party behind him, this is something I betted on not occurring when I was still confident in Rogers, Unfortunately the NE may just be blue enough to get him over the line but there is still time for that change so let's hope so.

Now for Ohio, this state is interesting in that so many people still seem not to realize that it's Husted and not Vivek that the state GOP is more worried about. To my shock, Husted (up until recently at least) has ran a pretty poor campaign and I believe the only reason he isn't down completely is because Brown's campaign has been equally subpar, just a very strange race overall, it's going to be closer than it should be but Husted will pull it out in the end doing a point or so worse than Moreno in 2024.

Now for the state I gave up on months ago, Georgia, things have only gotten worse for the Senate race here, I don't expect the bottom to completely fall out underneath Mike Collins but he's deeply underwater here and is still not running the campaign needed to keep it close. I've been massively overestimating KLB however and greatly underappreciating Jackson's efforts on the airwaves and on the trail, this race will not be close, I see Jackson winning 4-6 in the end.

I'm going to combine two states here, Texas and Kansas, I'll start with Kansas first. Marshall will be fine and will win by mid to high single digits at worse, his opponent's recent "surge" is the result of something I now like to call phantom momentum. The recent attention this race has gotten is purely the result of an immaterial "scandals" Marshall has had, paired with a bunch of Dem internals showing the race tightening or tied in under two months, it's possible Marshall underperforms but he will not lose.

Now for Texas and Ken Paxton, honestly the discourse around this race is near insufferable, Paxton isn't losing. Of course it will be tighter than it should be but the fundamentals still remain with Paxton, traditionally straight ticket voting R's aren't going to suddenly turn on the party nominee and vote for fucking Talarico because a deeply despised incumbent got crushed by 25! 

Or because Paxton had issues in his marriage in the past or whatever other "scandal" you want to insert here. Paxton has a good record as the state AG that is what is going to matter the most to people. Plus, Talarico's recent absence from the trail and past words and positions are still looming large over him not to mention his Crockett problem.

Abbott's section is going to be much shorter because of how laughable the idea is that he will come anywhere close to losing this year. Yes this is his 4th time running and that will drag his margin down but Abbott is still very popular within Texas, to believe Abbott is in danger of losing you have to believe he has magically become extremely unpopular in the past 6 months or that he is being dragged down by Paxton or French. Neither of which are true nor backed up by anything on the ground, the DGA have literally diverted resources away from Texas to defend Oregon lmao.

Now before we get to the margins, I have a very simple message I'd like to restate. If you want us to win, then get out and vote Republican up and down the ballot. If you truly can't stand whatever R is on the ballot in your state, then take a note from Trump and imagine yourself voting for him instead. This simple act is and will be the easiest and most effective way to achieve victory and get what you want in the next two years.

@ChristopherHale @nicksorter Why would Ken Paxton need someone to manufacture an elaborate hoax to benefit his campaign? What exactly would he stand to gain from orchestrating a story that could easily backfire if exposed as fraudulent?

#News A private jet based in Austin, Texas, flew to a small airport about 20 minutes from a well-known private inpatient mental health center in Ohio, then returned to Austin the next morning (yesterday) landing hours before James Talarico reappeared in public after almost two weeks of being 'missing' that his campaign blamed on the flu.

#austin
Public flight tracking confirms the aircraft’s flight between Austin and Butler County Regional Airport (HAO) in Hamilton, Ohio.

#Ohio
Rumors started circulating that Talarico's absence was due to a mental health breakdown, according to numerous sources, and his campaign flew out to retrieve him when the online chatter became too big to contain.

Details:
➡The plane is N750MF, a Cessna Citation X operated by Jet Linx Aviation and based in the Austin area.

➡TFlight data shows it left Austin for Hamilton, Ohio, on October 8 and returned the following morning, landing in Austin around 10:23 a.m. local time.

➡THamilton’s airport is a short drive from the Lindner Center of HOPE in Mason, Ohio - which is a private, nonprofit facility offering inpatient, residential, and outpatient psychiatric care for adults and adolescents.

➡TThis is the same center that Harris County Judge Lina Hidalgo checked herself into in 2023 and spent seven weeks at for mental health treatment. It cost about $88,000.

Talarico, who's running against Attorney General Ken Paxton for U.S. Senate, had not held an in-person campaign event in Texas since around September 26.

On September 30 he joined a Hispanic Business Council event virtually and said he had gone to urgent care in Dallas the night before:
Then he went 'missing.'

Campaign spokesman JT Ennis repeated the flu excuse and said Talarico would return to the trail over the weekend. He didn't.
On October 9, after the plane landed, Talarico appeared at the Austin City Limits Music Festival.

Ennis posted video and wrote that Talarico was “still alive and meeting with voters at ACL today.”

But people aren't buying the flu excuse saying the schedule doesn't match the timeline, and the flight from Austin to Ohio is too much of a coincidence.
Timeline:

🔵Tuesday, September 29, Greenwich Village, a second fundraiser, on his campaign’s invitation.

🔵A Tuesday night reception in Greenwich Village, New York and a Tuesday night urgent-care visit in Dallas is not the same thing.
The campaign hasn't given an explanation, proof of a flight, a timestamp, or even a clinic name.

➡️The Edinburg forum on September 30 went virtual.

➡️An Austin fundraiser set for Tuesday was scrapped.

Paxton’s campaign launched a tip line and circulated missing-person-style posters.

Donald Trump isn't wielding the Discombobulator against Iran.

He's using Iran AS a Discombobulator against the Uniparty.

Last week, there was a coordinated Narrative push by many of the major MSM outlets using Ken Paxton and his contentious Texas race as a fulcrum through which to attempt to engineer a public split between Donald Trump and the GOP ... that the boss might not mind anyway, as I’ve been writing about for months.

But that’s not the point of this particular take.

Instead, I want to take you through 24 hours of Info War deployments, moves and countermoves as a case study of how quickly said Info War moves, and how Trump always occupies the winning (meaning not losing) position, while all other players react to his gravity, even if they do so in advance.

For starters, the Paxton deployment (covered by Axios, The New York Times and Politico, among others) consisted of a series of Op Eds and special reports with timely-leaked audio clips alleging that Paxton has been bashing Trump at private donor events and campaign settings, and that the heart of Paxton’s frustrations with Trump orbits the President’s continued perpetuation of the Iran War, which we are told is extremely unpopular among the American people.

Now, whether or not Paxton believes this to be true is quite besides the point.

The point is, the media wants the People to believe that, IF the GOP loses the upcoming Midterm Elections, it will mark a repudiation of Trump’s second (or third) term agenda, while piling on intra-party pressure for him to abandon whatever mission he’s on early into 2027.

Later that same day, the Narrative evolved along pre-planned grounds, with a special report in The Atlantic claiming that Trump had tasked his MIL commanders to explore the possibility of re-opening kinetic conflict with the Iranian Regime in a major way BEFORE the Midterm inflection point.

This report was then picked up and washed through all the other aforementioned outlets.

Later that night, on the Devolution Power Hour, I gave a longer version of this take, while @patel_patriot quite presciently observed that Trump would probably debunk/block this story the very next day.

Which he did ...

The thing is, while Jon was right about Trump’s disarmament, and while it continues to demonstrate Trump’s control over the Narrative battlespace, my point from the night before remains.

That point?

That the Iran War Narrative represents the ultimate 2026 Sword of Damocles the enemy (both from without and from within the so-called MAGA coalition) believes they are holding over Trump’s head, but which he is actually holding over theirs.

After all, do you think Trump is going to tell you (or them) the truth of what he will or will not do, and WHEN he will or will not do it on social media?

Certainly he wouldn’t do so in the event the Iran War was as ‘real’ as we are told it is.

And even in my usual framing, he wouldn’t do so even if it was ‘fake’ in the way people like Chris Paul and I discuss it.

So, what are we left with using last week’s Paxton-Iranian PsyOp as a microcosm?

Trump and Trump alone knows what he will or will not do regarding the Iran War Narrative ... and the Iran War Narrative is the most powerful weapon HE has at his disposal when it comes to drawing the center of mass psychological and narrative gravity to HIM and away from any who would attempt to subvert him, no matter which ‘party’ they are publicly aligned with.

In the end, I believe Trump has been baiting the weaker elements within the GOP to break with him publicly before the Midterm inflection point, and I believe the Iran War narrative has been his most effective means in doing so, which is why he continues to alternatively escalate and de-escalate every day, every week and every month.

He’s not Discombobulating Iran.

He’s using Iran to Discombobulate the Uniparty.

The Iran War ended in June 2025, according to Trump himself.

What we’re watching is the legacy of those who would have perpetuated it echo in keeping with Trump’s desire to find out who is who when the going gets tough.

And the media may now accidentally be helping him do it.

In the end, I believe the Midterm Election cycle matters less in terms of deciding who occupies an illegitimate Congress, and much more in terms of who Trump knows he can trust and who he most decidedly cannot ahead of what could be the final two-year sprint of his Golden Age transition.

posts.text:
1/3
🚨 WATCH: MAGA uses bots to hack the ALGORITHM and REALITY, The James Talarico Story  PART 2 🚨

After the James Talarico post blew up, I did a follow-up analysis on the MAGA influencer sphere on Twitter. I adjusted the last chart to fit the new data, and came up with what I'm calling a “Music Drop visualization” to show something I only briefly covered last time. Repost bots.

In this post, you can see some of the biggest accounts outside Elon Musk, are MAGA “influencers” who are very high traffic on twitter, but don’t have much reach beyond it. https://t.co/zCUmg0TACm
credit: slendie (@DatBoiSlendie)

A small number of accounts drive an incredible amount of traffic with fairly crude bot networks as I will show. Over Oct 11 and 12, 294 accounts posted 1,575 word-for-word copies of just seven MAGA accounts. 134 of them copied Eric Daugherty 960 times, and every one of his 121 posts got copied. The busiest copier posted 141 copies in two days. All of these dots falling off the top line are mostly word for word copies of the original, and a smaller amount within 10% variance. This is nearly, if not 100% manufactured, and it works very well.

To pour some cold water on another theory that's been going around, I've also seen NO drop in post volume I could pin on the Russian data centres being hit. That's only from what I've seen on Twitter and on the topics I looked at, I can't speak for reddit or other topics outside maga. 

However, I think there is ANOTHER reason things feel different in the last few days. Algorithm changes. If I'm correct, algorithm changes explain more of the posting patterns and feed changes people have noticed or felt. Including what may have changed, and what to watch for from the MAGA accounts in the next month.  More on that below. 

For now, enjoy (headphones recommended).

posts.name: Louis Riel
posts.text:
2/3
HOW THEY DO IT

At 1:05 pm on Oct 11, Nick Sortor posted that an Ohio mental hospital "CONFIRMS" James Talarico was discharged. As on previous days, the bot network immediately began priming the algorithm by generating activity around what Nick was talking about.

• In the 10 minutes before his post, 26 posts named Talarico. In the half hour after, 762 did, from 620 accounts with 29.2M followers between them.
• 109 accounts were repeating the story within half an hour. 18 posted Sortor's own words.
• His post drew 6.2M views on its own, and his posts that day drew 7x his usual views.
• Posts pushing the "discharged" claim drew 14M views. The Lindner Center said at 7:47 pm that Talarico never received treatment there.
• On Oct 11 the first copy of a Talarico post came in 7 minutes, down from 42 the day before.

None of this slowed down when drones hit Yandex data centres on Oct 8, 9 and 11. I haven't seen a single traffic pattern on Twitter I can pin on the data centres. If anything I'm seeing more MAGA traffic, not less. It’s just now operating in a slightly different pattern in the last 4 days, something I suspect (but can’t prove), is changes to the algorithm and expanding their bot networks.

• The share of Talarico posts that were word-for-word copies climbed through the strike days, from 2.7 per 100 on Oct 7 to 5.5, 5.3 and 6.8.
• Eric Daugherty's copy network tripled, from 2.4 copies a post (mid-July to Oct 3) to 7.3 (Oct 6 to 12). The jump started Oct 4 to 6, before the first strike. His first copy now lands in 5 minutes, down from 22.
• Nick Sortor's copies rose by half, from 1.9 a post to 3.0, in spikes on Oct 6, 8 and 11.

The day after the Talarico story, during a Trump speech, @unclejerich0 caught the same machine live, a wall of accounts all posting "funniest president ever" about Trump at once. Credit to them:
https://t.co/qjc31ZUnIY

Two things explain all this better than the data centres. More bots, which I can measure, and possibly algorithm changes, which I can't, at least directly.

The algorithm part is some speculation, but I think it could also explain the "who turned off the bots?" feeling. Certain astroturfing methods, like one very dedicated small community driving a trend, are getting crowded out by the more crude and obvious bot farms.

Imagine a normal post that spreads on twitter outside of politics.  Fourth quarter, QB throws a duck that's intercepted. Hundreds or thousands of fans who don't know each other are all tweeting about it. That's what a real event looks like, and it should trend. My guess is X turned up the weight on exactly that, lots of accounts posting about the same thing at the same time, as opposed to more community driven narratives.

The swarm style of boosting, where a community of accounts that follow each other repost and reply to push a story (think of all the right wings “patriots” constantly retweeting eachother and brigading replies) seems to get less out of it now. It doesn't even need to be turned down.

It just gets squeezed out by the increased weight on the repost bots. The influence networks will quickly adapt to these new changes, and I suspect many patterns will return to the usual firehouse of bs within a week once everyone figures it out.

For now, repost bots look exactly like the football fans to the algorithm. Hundreds of accounts posting the same words within minutes sends the same signal as a stadium full of people yelling about sports (shoutout Luke Littler). The algo can't tell the difference.

Small Caveat, tripling Eric Daugherty's copy bots didn't triple his reach. His median views per post rose about 16%.

Where it does show up in the numbers, is the topic. The copying rate had been running at similar levels for days, yet once Sortor posted and all the MAGA bots all suddenly unified their messaging on it, the Talarico story went parabolic. 26 posts named Talarico in the 10 minutes before his post, then 762 in the half hour after, and the story finished the day 10x bigger than the day before (10,406 posts against 1,009). It trended in a way it usually doesn't and spread well beyond the communities those posts usually reach.

That fits my speculation that in recent days, the algorithm leans slightly more towards boosting a topic as a whole once enough accounts are posting about it independently, rather than boosting any single account.

The bots are not magic, and the algorithm piece is still my speculation, not something X has confirmed.

One thing that IS certain, is that this problem is only going to get worse int he next month.

posts.text:
Hidden GOP vote could ‘easily’ keep the Senate in Republican hands | Nick Givas, The Western Journal

CNN chief data analyst Harry Enten said Monday that Republicans have a substantial chance of maintaining their Senate majority if polling numbers are off by only a few points.

Enten pointed out that the polling industry has consistently favored Democrats in past elections and said it would not take much for the Republicans to hold on to vital toss-up seats.

“Let’s just say we have the 2026 Senate polls, but if the polls are underestimating the Republicans by 3.5 points, which you know is really possible, because we’ve seen it through the history, right? You go back to 2020, that’s basically what happened,” he declared.

“Even in 2024, in a number of the key states we saw it happen, including places like Texas.”

Enten then rattled off several other high-profile contests, some in ruby-red states, and said voters could easily defy pollsters and flip the blue wave narrative on its head.

“How about Michigan? How about up there in Maine, how about in Alaska, how about in Iowa, how about in Kansas — which has been getting a lot of press lately — all of these go red. All these go red, and the Republicans don’t just hold the United States Senate; they hold it easily with 52 seats to the Democrats’ 48 seats.”

Enten’s map didn’t even include potential GOP Senate wins in Ohio, North Carolina, New Hampshire, or Georgia, where Republicans have historically been competitive, if not outright dominant.

If polls are underestimating Republicans in the states that Enten mentioned, and they stay red, the GOP would only need to pick off two swing states to increase their current 53-47 majority.

The CNN analyst also highlighted how the early October generic congressional ballot has underestimated Republicans in 14 of 16 elections since 1994.

“What is going on here?” Enten asked. “And it’s happened by an average of, I believe, what is this — four points. The average is a four-point underestimation of Republicans since 1994.”

Democratic Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer of New York also raised concerns on Tuesday about GOP fundraising advantages, according to a letter obtained by The Hill.

Schumer wrote that control of the upper chamber could come down to an “unprecedented tsunami of Republican money” that has the potential to level the playing field in the home stretch, with only weeks to go until Election Day.

“We have strong candidates, a clear message, and a political climate that offers real opportunities. But Republicans have one enormous advantage of their own. Money,” Schumer stated.

He also said President Donald Trump has the bandwidth to spend between $400 million and $500 million through his super PAC, MAGA Inc., and that big tech mogul Elon Musk has pumped nearly $300 million into the midterm races to help Republican candidates.

Schumer added that other “megadonors” have jumped into the fray and are funding Senate races at rates unlike anything “we’ve ever seen before.”

“That’s the enormous force bearing down on this election,” Schumer concluded. “And it’s a challenge none of us can afford to underestimate.”
