posts.text:
An Open Letter to Arizona Voters Who Supported President Trump

To the Arizonans who voted for President Trump,

I grew up in rural Arizona, in Prescott, on a dirt road behind the world’s oldest rodeo. My parents taught my siblings and I to appreciate hard work and the beauty of this state. Today, I’m the first Mom to ever serve as Arizona’s Attorney General, after proudly serving two terms as a Republican on the Corporation Commission, where we stood up for consumers when powerful utilities went too far.

When I ran for Attorney General, I ran to represent all Arizonans. To be the Lawyer for the People. Not powerful corporations, not special interests, and not any political party. My job is to fight for the people of this state, whether you’re a Republican, Democrat, or Independent, whether you live in the Valley or in rural Arizona. And those aren’t just words – they are embodied by my record, our work inside the Attorney General’s Office.

First, let’s talk about fentanyl:

Arizonans want to keep dangerous drugs off our streets and protect our families. Alongside local police, sheriffs, and our federal law enforcement partners, my office has seized more than 27 million fentanyl pills, more than any Attorney General in Arizona history. We also fought to change the law to give law enforcement the tools to shoot down Mexican drug cartel drones transporting fentanyl, meth, and carfentanil across the border. Arizona law enforcement and federal agencies working here seize a massive share of the fentanyl recovered across the country, often accounting for more than half of all national seizures.  My office works hand in glove to make those seizures and prosecute 80 percent of the major cases and the cartels. That’s what it means to focus on the worst of the worst: go after the drug cartels, smugglers, and human traffickers who threaten our communities every day.

Second, let’s talk about the cost of living in Arizona:

You can feel it everywhere you go in this state. People are working harder than ever, but too many families still feel like they're falling behind: Groceries cost more, housing costs more, health care costs more, and utility bills keep going up. That’s why I fought to stop the Kroger-Albertsons merger that would have combined Frys and Safeway. Arizona families deserve competition and choices at the grocery store, not fewer companies with more power to increase prices. It’s why my office sued RealPage and corporate landlords over allegations they colluded to drive up rents in 76% of the apartment units in Phoenix and more than 50% of apartments in Tucson. And it’s why I intervened to challenge proposed electricity rate increases from APS and TEP.  When companies get so big they think the rules no longer apply to them, somebody has to stand up to them. That’s what I’ve done as Attorney General.

Third, let’s talk about Arizona’s water supplies:

Arizonans viscerally understand that we can’t keep doing dumb things with our water supply. It’s a threat to our families, our way of life, and our future. That’s why I sued the Saudi-owned megafarm pumping Arizona groundwater to grow alfalfa for export overseas to feed livestock in the Persian Gulf. While Arizona communities worry about dwindling groundwater, this foreign-owned corporation was taking advantage of our resources to serve its own interests. And it’s why I brought Riverview Dairy to the table in Cochise County to put up $11 million to redrill the wells of their neighbors and fallow thousands of acres of land in an effort to restore the aquifer there. Arizona’s water supply must be protected. It belongs to the people of this state, and I will keep fighting to defend it.

Those are the fights I’ll keep taking on if I’m reelected. I won’t stop because someone has more money, more power, or a different political affiliation. I know you may not agree with me on everything, and we didn’t vote the same way last election. But I’m asking you to trust that I’ll fight for you – because you’re an Arizonan.

This next term, I’ll fight to protect our water from foreign companies pumping it dry, will fight to ensure big data centers aren’t driving up your electric bills, will protect your privacy when companies like Flock invade it, and will investigate predatory surveillance pricing. Those aren’t partisan issues, they are our issues, our fights.

I also plan to continue to be the most transparent AG in history by getting out and talking to Arizonans.  I’ve done more town halls in the past four years – 60 plus of them – than any other AG.  Those town halls – from Benson to Chino Valley, from Wendon to St. Johns, from Pearce to Lake Havasu, from Yuma to Sierra Vista – have been the best part of my job, and they have helped us to investigate and tackle some of our toughest issues.

As your Attorney General I will always stand shoulder to shoulder with you – to protect our communities and ensure a future for our children in this state we all love.

Sincerely,
Kris Mayes, Arizona Attorney General

posts.name: Governor Mikie Sherrill
posts.text:
There has been a lot of discussion about Hegseth's plan to publicly execute Nidal Hasan, but not enough about what this means. Nidal Hasan killed 13 innocent soldiers and deserves to be brought to justice. But a televised public spectacle of an execution is contrary to the values that this nation stands for and that I took oaths to protect. It is hard to understand how Congress has not called an emergency session to block it.

One aspect of this in particular keeps me up at night: the horror of detailing soldiers to be in the firing squad. Most veterans like myself are unfamiliar with firing squads because our military hasn't used one in over 80 years. From my understanding, they are usually made up of three to seven personnel, with some rifles being loaded with blanks to "reduce psychological harm."

I think about my own kids serving in the military, and I imagine a young service member getting detailed to the firing squad, feeling they have to follow orders despite any moral objection or personal opposition. Just about anyone who has served in combat can tell you about the toll it takes. This is different and worse: firing on someone for the public spectacle of it.

It infuriates me that, in an ode to Trump and Hegseth's warped view of toughness, the United States would sanction a military firing squad simply for the pageantry of it — no matter how it harms our service members. It is disgusting that this Administration is essentially glorifying violence and death by firearm — something we already have too much of in this country. It infuriates me to think of all the Members of Congress who have thanked me for my service on Veterans Day, but have said nothing about this and refuse to hold Trump and Hegseth accountable. It infuriates me that soldiers will be scarred for life if this goes forward — for no other reason beyond Pete Hegseth's vanity.

I imagine the young person getting detailed to the firing squad and doing their duty, following their orders. And I think of the lasting impact that will have on them. I just wish the two men in charge of our military cared half as much about the men and women who serve as they do about themselves.

Trump cancels Hegseth’s plan to live-stream Fort Hood shooter’s execution

President Donald Trump rejected Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s plan to live-stream the execution by firing squad of Nidal Hasan, a former U.S. Army psychiatrist who killed numerous colleagues at Fort Hood, Texas, in 2009.

President Donald Trump on Thursday said that the forthcoming execution of a former U.S. Army psychiatrist who killed numerous colleagues at Fort Hood, Texas, in 2009 will not be live-streamed, upending a plan that Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth unveiled last week.

Nidal Malik Hasan will still be put to death, but “this event will not be streamed,” Trump said in a social media post.

“I think streaming the execution for all to see might have been a strong deterrent for the World to witness how America deals with Terrorists and SCUM like Hasan but, many very good and well meaning people would rather not watch him die, through streaming, or through any other visual device,” Trump said.

MIDTERMS — MON PRONOSTIC SÉNAT ÉVOLUE et beaucoup ne vont pas aimer...

▶️ Le 2 septembre, j’avais 49 républicains, 50 démocrates et l’Alaska indécidable. Au 15 octobre, je passe à 50 républicains, 49 démocrates, Alaska toujours indécidable. Pourquoi ? Je réévalue le Texas et l’Ohio, que j’avais placés en bleu.

▶️ Ce n’est pas parce que les sondages se seraient brutalement retournés. C’est précisément parce que je veux moins dépendre des sondages. Texas et Ohio sont exactement les deux endroits de ma carte où une petite avance démocrate dans les enquêtes suppose aujourd’hui un décrochage important par rapport aux fondamentaux électoraux récents.

▶️ J'ajoute un deuxième élément : la participation. Les démocrates disposent d'un avantage considérable chez les jeunes électeurs, mais ceux-ci votent historiquement moins régulièrement lors des élections de mi-mandat que les électeurs plus âgés. Une intention de vote n'a de valeur électorale que si elle devient un bulletin.

▶️ Et nous commençons justement à disposer d'un troisième indicateur : le vote anticipé. Je le suis désormais quotidiennement. Il montre bien une mobilisation démocrate — elle est même particulièrement visible dans l'Ohio — mais, à l'échelle des États où nous disposons déjà de données, je ne vois pas encore de raison de transformer la dynamique spectaculaire observée dans certains sondages en gain électoral acquis. Les premiers votes sont un indicateur de participation, pas un résultat, et leur composition doit être interprétée État par État. 

▶️ C'est important parce que les enquêtes nationales décrivent actuellement un environnement exceptionnellement favorable aux démocrates : ils devancent les républicains de 8 points dans le vote générique de Pew et leur avantage est encore plus considérable parmi les électeurs se déclarant les plus motivés. Mais lorsque Pew regarde les électeurs ayant effectivement voté en 2022 et en 2024, l'avantage démocrate se réduit à 6 points. C'est exactement le genre d'écart qui m'incite aujourd'hui à la prudence. 

▶️ Enfin, il reste les fondamentaux géographiques. Pour reprendre le Sénat, les démocrates doivent notamment gagner des sièges dans des États que Trump avait remportés à deux chiffres en 2024. Texas et Ohio ne deviennent pas mécaniquement bleus parce que l'environnement national est très favorable aux démocrates. 

▶️ Je préfère donc appliquer ma méthode jusqu’au bout : fondamentaux > sondages.
🔴 Texas : D → R
🔴 Ohio : D → R
🟤 Alaska : toujours impossible à définir

Cela ne signifie évidemment pas que Talarico ou Brown ne peuvent pas gagner. Ils le peuvent — et l'Ohio me paraît aujourd'hui le plus susceptible de me donner tort. Cela signifie que, si je dois faire un pronostic aujourd'hui, leurs quelques points d'avance dans les sondages ne suffisent plus à me faire ignorer le terrain sur lequel ils courent, la participation qui reste à matérialiser et les incertitudes propres aux sondages.

➡️ Mon pronostic au 15 octobre : GOP 50 — Démocrates 49 — Alaska indécidable.
Et c’est aussi pour cela qu’un pronostic doit pouvoir changer : il ne s’agit pas de défendre sa carte du mois dernier, mais d’essayer d’avoir la bonne le 3 novembre. 

▶️ Je sens que je vais adorer vos commentaires...😘

TRUMP CANCELS PLANS TO LIVESTREAM FORT HOOD SHOOTER’S EXECUTION

President Donald Trump announced Thursday that the execution of Nidal Malik Hasan will no longer be broadcast to the public.

Hasan, a former U.S. Army psychiatrist, was convicted of murdering 13 people and wounding 32 others during the November 5, 2009, mass shooting at Fort Hood, Texas.

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth had proposed livestreaming Hasan’s execution by firing squad as a public demonstration of justice and deterrence.

However, the proposal sparked bipartisan criticism, including objections from Vice President JD Vance, military veterans, religious leaders, and victims’ families.

A recent Washington Post–ABC News–Ipsos poll found that 80% of Americans opposed broadcasting the execution.

Trump confirmed that Hasan’s execution remains scheduled for December 3, 2026, but only immediate family members of the victims will be permitted to witness it in person.

If carried out, it would be the first U.S. military execution since 1961.

Do you agree with Trump’s decision, or should the execution be broadcast publicly?

posts.text:
El presidente de Estados Unidos, Donald Trump, canceló el plan de transmitir en vivo la ejecución de Nidal Malik Hasan, un exmilitar condenado a muerte por asesinar a 13 personas durante un tiroteo en Fort Hood, Texas, en 2009.

La decisión llega después de una ola de críticas de republicanos, demócratas, organizaciones de derechos humanos y líderes religiosos.

¿Qué ocurrió?

La masacre: El 5 de noviembre de 2009, Hasan, entonces psiquiatra del Ejército estadounidense, abrió fuego contra militares en la base de Fort Hood. El ataque dejó 13 muertos y 32 heridos.

La condena: En 2013 fue sentenciado a muerte. Su ejecución por pelotón de fusilamiento está programada para el 3 de diciembre de 2026.

• El polémico anuncio: El secretario de Defensa, Pete Hegseth, había anunciado que la ejecución sería pública y el Pentágono confirmó que se transmitiría en directo.

• El rechazo: La propuesta provocó críticas incluso dentro del propio Gobierno. El vicepresidente JD Vance aseguró que no vería la transmisión, mientras que líderes religiosos y organismos internacionales cuestionaron la medida.

• La decisión final: Trump anunció que el fusilamiento seguirá programado, pero no será transmitido por internet ni televisión. Los familiares directos de las víctimas podrán presenciarlo si así lo desean.

Trump defendió inicialmente la transmisión porque consideraba que podía servir como advertencia para posibles terroristas, aunque reconoció que muchas personas preferirían no presenciar la muerte de Hasan.

El debate va más allá de este caso: La controversia reavivó la discusión sobre la pena de muerte, los límites del castigo estatal y las consecuencias de convertir una ejecución en un espectáculo público.

De concretarse, sería la primera ejecución militar estadounidense por fusilamiento desde la Segunda Guerra Mundial.

While Big Bend's border wall is tied up in a major legal fight right now, there's a bigger story hiding behind it: millions of acres of Texas public land.

The Texas General Land Office owns a massive checkerboard of parcels across the exact border counties, Hudspeth, Presidio, and Brewster, where the wall and vehicle barriers are planned. This isn't just any state land, it's Permanent School Fund (PSF) land, over 13 million acres constitutionally dedicated to funding Texas public schools.

It's leased out in scattered pieces, acre by acre, mostly to ranchers and oil and gas. Ranchers depend on it for water access. River guides depend on it for their livelihoods. Billy Miller, a river guide and landowner, testified at the October 2 hearing. Asked what Big Bend means to him, he said: "The wilderness of Big Bend saved my life."

So who's supposed to be protecting this land? Commissioner Dawn Buckingham runs the @TXGLO She spoke out once in July, after contractors cleared GLO land without permission. Since then, silence.

Turns out there's a reason. A reporter requested GLO's communications with the federal agency building the wall. GLO tried to keep it secret, but Texas law required them to show their own excuse to the reporter. It backfired: the letter admitted GLO's been in "regular contact" with CBP the whole time.

This isn't a neutral official caught in the middle. Buckingham publicly pledged to help Trump's deportation push by donating state land. Trump has endorsed her. She calls herself a "staunch defender of the Trump agenda." Her biggest donors are oil, gas, and ranching interests, the same industries leasing this land. Her July objection wasn't about protecting ranchers. It was lip service.

A wall that disrupts these leases doesn't just hurt ranchers, it threatens money meant for Texas kids. This administration has already cut Medicaid, SNAP, and school meal funding. Vanity projects over kids. That's the pattern.

Alex Gibney’s new documentary “Musk” paints Elon Musk as a man who sees other people as characters in his own video game, according to a review in The New Republic. 

The film, from the director of “Enron: The Smartest Guys in the Room” and “Going Clear,” runs nearly four hours with an intermission. 

Musk refused to be interviewed and instead called Gibney a “douche” on X, so Gibney built a database of Musk’s recorded interviews and created a computer-generated Musk avatar that “answers” questions using things Musk has actually said. 

The device plays on Musk’s long-held belief that life is probably a simulation, and the film portrays him as the main character in a digital world where everyone else is a “non-player character.” 

Reviewer David Klion describes the portrait that emerges as one of “an empty, hateful, emotionally stunted man” whose two superpowers are shameless self-promotion and an ability to exploit weaknesses in government regulation. 

The central question of the film, Klion writes, is how someone like Musk gained such immense power and “what does it say about the rest of us that we allowed it to happen?”

The documentary traces the damage Musk has done, from Tesla’s self-driving crashes to the dismantling of USAID, and includes his power over Ukraine’s battlefield through Starlink. 

Gibney interviews more than a dozen people, including Tesla co-founder Martin Eberhard, Musk’s ex-wife Justine, Ashley St. Clair, former USAID chief Samantha Power and members of Musk’s own family. 

The film highlights a Florida lawyer suing Tesla over its self-driving cars, which have been involved in at least 60 deaths. 

It also covers Musk’s gutting of the federal government through DOGE, and Power chokes up on camera describing the suffering caused to the world’s poorest people when USAID was dismantled. 

Gibney shows how Musk built ties with Trump, Argentina’s Javier Milei, Brazil’s Jair Bolsonaro and Turkey’s Recep Tayyip Erdogan to expand businesses like Starlink, which lets him “sway the battlefields of Ukraine by denying or granting access.” 

St. Clair, the mother of one of his 14 known children, says on camera that she refused to sign a nondisclosure agreement she claims Musk has offered other women and details the harassment she has faced since speaking out."

President Trump used a campaign stop for Ken Paxton this week to go after the man standing between him and a 32-year Republican flip of a Texas Senate seat: Democrat state Rep. James Talarico. Trump's nickname for him going in was 𝐓𝐚𝐥𝐚𝐟𝐫𝐞𝐚𝐤𝐨. Asked about it beforehand, Trump put it plainly: “𝘏𝘦 𝘪𝘴 𝘢 𝘭𝘪𝘵𝘵𝘭𝘦 𝘧𝘳𝘦𝘢𝘬𝘺” (TNND wire).

He didn't stop there once he reached the rally. “𝘐 𝘵𝘩𝘪𝘯𝘬 𝘩𝘦'𝘴 𝘢 𝘧𝘳𝘦𝘢𝘬. 𝘛𝘩𝘦𝘳𝘦'𝘴 𝘴𝘰𝘮𝘦𝘵𝘩𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘸𝘳𝘰𝘯𝘨 𝘸𝘪𝘵𝘩 𝘵𝘩𝘢𝘵 𝘨𝘶𝘺. 𝘈𝘯𝘥 𝘛𝘦𝘹𝘢𝘴 𝘤𝘢𝘯'𝘵 𝘩𝘢𝘷𝘦 𝘵𝘩𝘢𝘵 — 𝘩𝘦 𝘸𝘪𝘭𝘭 𝘣𝘦 𝘢𝘨𝘢𝘪𝘯𝘴𝘵 𝘺𝘰𝘶𝘳 𝘚𝘦𝘤𝘰𝘯𝘥 𝘈𝘮𝘦𝘯𝘥𝘮𝘦𝘯𝘵.” Trump also went after Talarico's record on women's sports, saying he's “𝘵𝘰𝘵𝘢𝘭𝘭𝘺 𝘪𝘯 𝘧𝘢𝘷𝘰𝘳 𝘰𝘧 𝘮𝘦𝘯 𝘱𝘭𝘢𝘺𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘪𝘯 𝘸𝘰𝘮𝘦𝘯'𝘴 𝘴𝘱𝘰𝘳𝘵𝘴”.

Then came Paxton's favorite attack line — that the Austin lawmaker is secretly vegan in cattle-and-barbecue country. “𝘏𝘦'𝘴 𝘢 𝘷𝘦𝘨𝘢𝘯 — 𝘢𝘭𝘭 𝘰𝘧 𝘢 𝘴𝘶𝘥𝘥𝘦𝘯 𝘩𝘦'𝘴 𝘨𝘰𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘵𝘰 𝘣𝘢𝘳𝘣𝘦𝘤𝘶𝘦𝘴, 𝘦𝘢𝘵𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘮𝘦𝘢𝘵, 𝘢𝘯𝘥 𝘵𝘩𝘳𝘰𝘸𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘶𝘱 𝘵𝘸𝘰 𝘮𝘪𝘯𝘶𝘵𝘦𝘴 𝘭𝘢𝘵𝘦𝘳 𝘢𝘵 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘣𝘢𝘤𝘬 𝘰𝘧 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘤𝘰𝘶𝘯𝘵𝘦𝘳”, Trump said. It's a good line, but 𝐏𝐨𝐥𝐢𝐭𝐢𝐅𝐚𝐜𝐭 𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐮𝐧𝐝𝐞𝐫𝐥𝐲𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐯𝐞𝐠𝐚𝐧 𝐜𝐥𝐚𝐢𝐦 𝐟𝐚𝐥𝐬𝐞: Talarico has been photographed eating meat on the trail, and his campaign says he “𝘪𝘴 𝘯𝘰𝘵 𝘢𝘯𝘥 𝘯𝘦𝘷𝘦𝘳 𝘩𝘢𝘴 𝘣𝘦𝘦𝘯 𝘢 𝘷𝘦𝘨𝘢𝘯 𝘰𝘳 𝘷𝘦𝘨𝘦𝘵𝘢𝘳𝘪𝘢𝘯” (PolitiFact).

Where Trump isn't exaggerating is the money. Talarico has 𝐨𝐮𝐭-𝐫𝐚𝐢𝐬𝐞𝐝 𝐏𝐚𝐱𝐭𝐨𝐧 𝐫𝐨𝐮𝐠𝐡𝐥𝐲 𝟑-𝐭𝐨-𝟏, pulling in $𝟑𝟏.𝟗 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐭𝐨 𝐏𝐚𝐱𝐭𝐨𝐧’𝐬 $𝟗.𝟏 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧 in FEC filings, with nearly half of it coming from outside Texas — led by California and New York donors (Newsweek). FBI Disrupts North Korean Corporate Espionage Ring in North Texas | Bethany Blankley, The Center Square

FBI agents in north Texas have disrupted a North Korean espionage ring targeting U.S. companies. The scheme involves illegally obtaining information from U.S. companies to facilitate the country’s sanctioned weapons program, federal authorities allege.

The case “is about far more than fraud,” U.S. Attorney Ryan Raybould for the Northern District of Texas said. “It is about a hostile foreign regime infiltrating American companies through stolen identities and covert access points inside our own borders.”

Federal agents disrupted what they describe as “a major illicit laptop‑hosting network” that enabled North Korean IT workers to unlawfully access U.S. corporate systems using stolen or falsified American identities for the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea (DPRK), authorities said. The U.S. has designated DPRK as a state sponsor of terrorism.

The bust was made through a federal Operation Lonestar Roundup with the assistance of the U.S. cybersecurity firm CrowdStrike. FBI special agents executed searches at more than 40 residences in Texas, seizing 187 laptops and keyboards, video and mouse devices. The devices were used as part of a “laptop farm” for DPRK IT workers, according to the complaint.

The majority were seized in north Texas. FBI agents seized approximately 100 devices that DPRK workers and their U.S.-based facilitators used to carry out the fraudulent scheme in north Texas, authorities said. The laptop farm was established to obtain remote employment and generate revenue for the DPRK’s sanctioned weapons programs, authorities allege.

“Every laptop farm we dismantle shuts down a revenue stream that the North Korean government relies on to fund weapons programs that threaten global stability,” Raybould said. “Operation Lonestar Roundup sends a clear message: we will not allow enemies of the United States to exploit our businesses or compromise our national security.”

Operation Lonestar Roundup in Texas was launched to disrupt “malicious cyber activity perpetrated by the North Korean government with the purpose of supporting its WMD and ballistic missile programs, intelligence program, and nuclear program,” FBI Dallas Special Agent in Charge Joseph Rothrock said. “Each laptop seized potentially represents one company that has hired a DPRK IT worker.”

According to investigative findings, DPRK IT workers applied for and obtained remote positions at U.S. companies by using stolen or fabricated identity documents, virtual private networks and proxy infrastructure. The scheme made it seem as if they were physically located in the U.S. but were instead in North Korea, according to the complaint. To do this, they relied on U.S.-based facilitators “who received laptops from victim companies, housed and configured those devices, installed remote-access software and transferred earnings to DPRK‑controlled accounts,” according to the complaint.

CrowdStrike has been working with the FBI to target DPRK operatives nationwide. In late September, it says its Counter Adversary Operations team collaborated with the FBI to disrupt several laptop farms operating nationwide maintained by DPRK-nexus adversary FAMOUS CHOLLIMA. Between April and June, its team identified the infrastructure, it says.

FAMOUS CHOLLIMA is a North Korean state-sponsored hacking group involved in fraudulent IT-worker schemes that has been active since at least 2018, CrowdStrike says. It “likely conducts operations on behalf of North Korea’s Munitions Industry Department (MID), which funds and oversees the DPRK’s missile and nuclear weapons program.”

The scheme involves DPRK operatives using laptop farms to enable FAMOUS CHOLLIMA operatives “to pose as legitimate remote workers and siphon illicit wages back to their regime while maintaining persistent access to victim organizations” in the U.S.. authorities allege.

In north Texas, investigators said they uncovered DPRK operatives using a network of fraudulent Google email accounts to facilitate the scheme. The DOJ published the emails in the complaint.

The bust comes as the Trump administration’s FBI is aggressively pursuing cybercrimes and corporate espionage. These investigations are an outworking of National Security Presidential Memorandum 11 (NSPM-11) issued to advance American superiority in artificial intelligence technology.

A federal investigation into DPRK illicit financial networks is ongoing.

The FBI is encouraging any company or individual who has information about the DPRK scheme to come forward and file a report at https://t.co/QZ2gHXHZ8n.

posts.text:
A bigger sample doesn’t fix a bad poll.

I joined fellow pollster John McLaughlin (@jmclghln) on @NEWSMAX’s National Report to explain why the most important question isn’t simply how many people answered a poll. It’s how they conducted the poll, who answered, AND who was missed.

McLaughlin offered a striking example: A Texas survey had far more respondents recalling voting for Kamala Harris than actually did, in a state that strongly backed Trump.

That’s why good reporters need to start examining the methodology, not just write a headline.

I explained why American Pulse uses multiple ways to reach people: live telephone interviews, text surveys, and other modes. Someone who ignores a call may answer a text. Different methods help reach different people.

Then look underneath the numbers: Are they surveying likely voters? Are postgraduate respondents overrepresented—a common problem? And most importantly, does the sample’s recalled 2024 presidential vote reasonably reflect what actually happened?

For pollsters whose livelihoods depend on getting it right, those aren’t academic questions. They’re essential checks and should be for reporters too.

Getting it right is a very different incentive from producing cheap, drive-by media polls to grab headlines.

Before trusting a poll’s take on the next election, let’s look at what it says happened in the last one.

Thanks to anchors @E_D_Hill and @KyleLowder, @jmclghln, @NEWSMAX, and the excellent National Report team for the opportunity to pull back the curtain on what good polls actually look like.

This was rare, next-level news coverage. Kudos.

posts.name: GET A GRIP
posts.text:
🚨 Who’s gonna stop him?

A clip of JD Vance is circulating on @X (below) in which the vice president appears to say that the president “has a lot of authority” and then asks, “who’s going to stop him?” It’s been shared thousands of times as proof that Vance believes Trump is beyond the reach of any check or balance.

I’m afraid that version is misleading. But what Vance actually said, in the opening minutes of the interview the clip comes from, is more revealing, and in some ways far more worrying.

The remarks come from Vance’s appearance on The Sean Spicer Show, recorded in the VP’s ceremonial office at the @WhiteHouse and released on 16 October. Spicer asked what Vance had learned about government in two years as a senator and two as VP. Vance replied that “so much of the power in our government does flow from the president”, before turning to his years in the Senate:

“But fundamentally, the president just has a lot of authority. And you realize that in government, when you’re in the United States Senate, you’re like, how is it that he is quite literally illegally opening the American southern border? And the reality is because who’s going to stop him, right? The courts aren’t going to stop him.”

The “him” is Joe Biden, not Donald Trump. Vance was complaining about a president he opposed, not boasting about the one he serves. Anyone sharing the clip as evidence that Vance thinks Trump is unstoppable is misrepresenting him, and it gives his defenders an easy way to wave away a far more serious problem.

That problem sits a few seconds earlier. Comparing the American presidency with the governments of China and Russia, Vance said that power in Washington is far more concentrated, and then added: “When Joe Biden is the president, that’s [a] bad thing. When Donald Trump is the president, that’s a good thing.”

"Those are my principles, and if you don't like them... well, I have others" - attributed to Coucho Marx

The constitutional limits on the presidency exist because nobody can know who will hold the office next. A principle that applies only when the other side is in power is not a principle at all. Vance is describing an office with enormous authority and judging whether that authority is acceptable purely by who occupies it.

He confirmed as much a few minutes later. Asked about the border, he said: “We didn’t just talk about closing the border. We actually did it.” The same presidential power over the border that was “quite literally illegal” in Biden’s hands becomes, in Trump’s, a promise kept.

Vance’s central factual claim also needs examining. The courts did stop Biden on immigration where his actions were challenged as unlawful, and often quickly. Within a week of Biden’s inauguration, a federal judge in Texas blocked his 100-day pause on deportations, finding the administration had failed to justify it.

In March 2023, in Florida v United States, Judge Kent Wetherell ruled that Biden’s “Parole Plus Alternatives to Detention” policy breached immigration law and the required procedures, and struck it down nationwide. When the administration asked him to suspend that ruling pending appeal, he refused within a day, calling the request “borderline frivolous”. The appeal court also declined to step in.

None of this reversed the overall direction of Biden’s border policy, and encounters at the southern border reached record levels during his term. But that gap reflects what courts are for. Judges decide whether a policy is lawful, not whether it is wise.

When Texas challenged Biden’s decision to end Trump’s “Remain in Mexico” policy, the Supreme Court ruled in Biden v Texas in 2022 that he was entitled to end it. A lawful policy that Vance dislikes is a matter for Congress and the voters. Calling it “quite literally illegal” turns a political disagreement into a legal accusation and makes the courts’ refusal to share his view look like impotence.

Courts struck down particular policies on statutory and procedural grounds, which is the ordinary business of administrative law. None found that Biden had deliberately opened the border.

The deeper difficulty is that Vance’s complaint about the courts sits awkwardly beside everything else he has said about them. In a 2021 podcast interview he advised Trump to fire “every civil servant in the administrative state” and replace them “with our people”, adding that when the courts stop you, you should “stand before the country like Andrew Jackson did and say: ‘The chief justice has made his ruling. Now let him enforce it.’” (Jackson almost certainly never said it.)

Asked on ABC’s This Week in February 2024 whether a president could defy the Supreme Court, he said yes, if the ruling cut into the president’s legitimate powers.

And in February 2025, with courts blocking parts of Trump’s agenda, he wrote that “judges aren’t allowed to control the executive’s legitimate power.”

Put those statements next to the Spicer interview and the pattern is plain. When a Democratic president governs, the failure of the courts to stop him is a scandal. When a Republican president governs, judges who try to stop him are overstepping, and he may be entitled to ignore them. The courts are a check for one side only.

There is a more serious version of Vance’s argument, and it deserves an answer. It holds that the modern administrative state has grown beyond democratic control, that unelected officials and judges can frustrate an elected president, and that real accountability requires the president to command the executive branch. This “unitary executive” theory has respectable defenders in American legal thought.

It is also true that politicians of both parties tend to rediscover the virtues of executive restraint when they lose power.

But someone who held that view on principle would accept the same powers in an opponent’s hands, and Vance says plainly that he does not. He presents his position on the courts as defending the president’s constitutional authority against judicial overreach.

The difficulty is that someone has to decide where legitimate executive power ends, and his proposed remedy when a court disagrees is defiance. On that account, the president becomes the final judge of his own limits. American democracy already has ways of holding a president to account: elections, Congress and the courts. A theory in which the president settles the limits of his own power removes the last of these.

This is a textbook case of what the discourse analyst Teun van Dijk calls the ideological square. Speakers emphasise the bad actions of the out-group and the good actions of the in-group, while playing down the in-group’s bad actions and the out-group’s good ones.

According to Vance, Biden’s use of presidential power is “quite literally illegal”, while under Trump the president simply “makes all the decisions”.

Later in the same interview Vance applied the same treatment to an individual opponent, telling Ohio voters that the Democratic Senate candidate Sherrod Brown “helped poison your neighbours and your neighbours kids with fentanyl because he was the person inviting those drug cartels into our country”.

Wildly hyperbolic claims like this aren’t unusual in political campaign rhetoric, but the mechanism is worth noticing: a political opponent’s record on immigration becomes personal responsibility for poisoning children. 

What drops out of view is that Brown steered the bipartisan FEND Off Fentanyl Act into law in 2024, which declared fentanyl trafficking a national emergency and expanded sanctions on Mexican cartels and Chinese chemical suppliers.

The rest of the opening passage fills out the picture. Vance noted, with something close to frustration, that China and Russia are “dictatorial” in terms of elections but “so bureaucratic” that decisions are made very slowly. The American presidency, by contrast, can simply act.

This is an odd and concerning and thing for a US VP to dwell on. The bureaucracy he dismisses, with its legal requirements, procedures and career officials, is part of what restrains arbitrary power. The rulings against Biden turned precisely on those requirements.

Then comes the familiar enemy. Biden’s White House, Vance said, was “staff-driven”, and a country without an active president ends up “run by the bureaucracy, run by the deep state”. Under Trump, by contrast, “the president makes all the decisions”.

There are genuine questions about how far career officials should be able to slow down an elected government. But the phrase “deep state” goes well beyond them, recasting a civil service bound by law as a mysterious hidden opponent.

The ideal Vance implies is a presidency where one man decides everything and the people who might tell him a policy is ineffective, immoral or unlawful have been cleared out of the way, which is exactly what Vance recommended in 2021.

There’s also deep irony here. Towards the end of the interview, Vance complained that reporters ask him to disavow things Trump has said, only for him to find that “you’re lying about what he said”. He insisted he does not let the media put words into anybody’s mouth. The viral clip did precisely that to Vance himself. But the answer to a distorted clip is to read what he actually said, and on this occasion his own words are damning enough.

Of course, none of this is new for a man who, in a private message in 2016, said he went back and forth between thinking Trump was a cynical Nixon type and “America’s Hitler”. What is new is how relaxed he sounds saying it, in the White House, a fortnight before the midterms, and with a 2028 run widely expected.

The viral clip misrepresents his words. His actual words set out a theory of government in which presidential power is good or bad according to who holds it, the civil service is an obstacle, and the courts are there to restrain his opponents. 

That deserves far more attention than a misleading ten-second clip.

Full interview:

posts.text:
Travel pool report 8: rest of rally

"I'm the king of the wall," Trump says, pointing to the rally regular in the "wall" suit in the front row. "By the way, Mexico did pay for that wall. I charged them tariffs and I charged them costs like they've never paid in history."

Trump references renaming of Gulf of Mexico to Gulf of America, crowd cheers.

Says he couldn't have done some things in the first term he's done in the second. "This is a much more powerful term, I can do stuff that's almost unbelievable."

"Canada has taken advantage of us for 50 years." "We lose "$90 billion a year…at some point we're making a year." Trudeau is "not a good guy.. a loser." "Your current guy is nice, but he's not good at trade." Says Canada "spends our money" on a health care system they shouldn't have.

Talks up the Senate race in North Carolina. Calls former Gov. Roy Cooper a "radical left governor, he's a lunatic." References the Willie Horton case from the Dukakis campaign. Relates it to Cooper, who he says let 88 murderers out of prison "because he didn't want them to catch COVID." Says "you should vote for Michael Whatley," the former RNC chair. Calls Whatley a "mental killer." "You should go out and work for him"

He repeated claims of fraud in the 2020 election in Georgia and Pennsylvania, saying "hundreds of boxes of ballots just happened to be found."

Talks about "transgender mutilization" and "open borders."
"Joe Biden and his whole group of crooks handed us the dark age of America. It was the dark age and they weaponized our government."

"We're in the golden age of America. Our nation is doing better than ever. But the fake news refuses to acknowledge it…. It was just announced that under Republican leadership, incomes have soared to the highest level ever."

"Remember Biden? 'It's great to be in Florida,' and he was in Maine."…"President Xi was here last week, and they respect our country."

"More Americans are working today than at any time in the history of our country." Says federal workers hated him but now they like him because they went out and got private sector jobs…. "I let over a million [federal workers] go." Says they've gotten better jobs, "they [women] get much more turned on" by their husbands who now make more money.

"Poverty rate has just reached the best number we've ever had."

"Stock market has hit 88 all-time highs" since the election, good news for 401k's. Asks folks to raise their hand if they have 401k. Many hands go up.

Riffs on "Barack Hussein Obama," and how Rush Limbaugh used to call him that.

"The Republican Party is starting to look pretty good…. latest poll says Ken Paxton is now leading in Texas. He's the greatest attorney general in the history of Texas." "The other guy's a freak."

Talks about how Melania is correcting his pronunciation of "vegan" and telling him not to dance. "She says, you are the president of the United States, you don't dance off the stage."

Why he's campaigning ahead of midterms: "I have to, because if they win the midterms, all you'll see is a slide."
"That's why iIm here, working my ass off for you."

"If you had a hat, if you bought a Make America Great again, you were under investigation by deranged Jack Smith."

Announces that if the Republicans win, the Department of War will be investing $100 million in the pharmaceutical company Anthea in Winchester, Kentucky.

"They're going to gut the Dept of War." "I rebuilt the military in the first term, then gave a lot of it away to Ukraine."

"If Republicans win the House and Senate, I'm going to give all adult citizens in the US $5,000. Only Republicans can do that, he says, because we're taking in massive amounts of money thru tariffs." He acknowledges it would cost US $1 trillion, but "we have $21 trillion coming in." Only caveat: You have to spend the money in the US. Jokes they can spend it at Mar a Lago one hamburger and a small dessert will cost about $5,000, he jokes.

Says Dems will raise your taxes and they're bragging about it. "Or you can defeat the Dumocrat communists, and get more money in your pockets." "No amnesty for illegal aliens."

"Just think of what we've accomplished in less than 2 years' time…We've inherited the worst border…and turned it into the strongest border. In the past 17 months, zero illegal aliens have been admitted into the United States." Talks about a case in Moorhead Kentucky and Louisville's "horrible sanctuary city policy." "If you vote for Andy Barr and a Republican Congress, we will end sanctuary cities."

Talks about "clean beautiful coal." On drug prices: "We went from paying the highest drug prices to the lowest"

Riffs on social and cultural issues transgender, making English the official language of the US. Talks about winning affirmative action case in SCOTUS.
"Iran will never have a nuclear weapon…that should have happened years ago."

"There's never been two years like this anywhere in the history of our country." "Construction numbers are thru the roof," he says, touting US economy. "We're leading in SI, we're building our pharmaceutical…" "Now the radical left Dumocrats want to burn it down." Attacks Democrats on a variety of issues, including no tax on tips, voter ID and proof of citizenship to vote.

"On election night, KY is going to prove that America does not belong to those who hate it, America belongs to those who really love it."

Goes after Michigan Democratic Senate nominee, misstates his name as "Mohamed El-Sayed." "I'm the president of the United States, I can call you whatever the hell I want."

At 3:31 pm, Trump invites Andy Barr to come up to the stage. "Kentucky loves President Donald Trump!" Barr says. Thanks Trump for investing in Kentucky "to power America." "This president believes in American energy dominance." Barr leaves the stage at 3:33 pm.

At 3:36 invites Ed Gallrein, R nominee for House, to the stage, after trashing outgoing GOP Rep. Thomas Massie, whom Gallrein defeated in the primary. "One year ago today he invited me to Oval Office," Gallrein said. He called on the audience to "help me with this no-fail mission." Went back to his seat at 3:37.

"We've done 9, maybe 10 of these in the last few days," he said, referring to political rallies. "They're saying something's happening these big monster rallies," in Montana, Alaska. "They're all watching, Ohio is watching. The spirit is incredible, it's infectious."

re the blue wave, and history of president's party doing poorly in midterms: "We're at, out of 25 races, a sitting president has won 2. There's never been any president that campaigned like this for the midterms…. If I don't make it, they're gonna get me. If we win, I will get absolutely no credit….

Shows video of Harry Enten on CNN talking about "MAGA GOP Voting Patterns." And how MAGA has stuck with Trump. And that he's more popular than Abraham Lincoln among MAGA voters.

Talks against $5,000 if R's win, promises to make the tax cuts permanent, make permanent the estate taxes, "we'll win the war on corruption and fraud," led by JD Vance; promises to prevent any future president from opening borders.

From earlier in the rally, courtesy of co-pooler Kerry Picket of WashTimes:
"Seventeen days from now. The people of Kentucky are going to defeat the radical left Democrat Charles Booker."
(on Andy Barr): "I backed him from day one when he was running for Congress against a very tough opponent."
(on Barr's chances): "I know all you'd have to do if the people turn out just a little bit, you're going to walk away, but you're going to have one of the best senators in Washington."
(on Ed Gallrein, who defeated Rep. Massie in GOP primary): "I looked at him walk through the door of the Oval Office. I said, that guy is central casting…He's a Navy seal, straight up and down." "here in Kentucky's 4th district, we're going to send Ed Gallrein to the US House of Representatives."

Rally ended at 3:50. YMCA is playing as pool files out

Linda Feldmann
The Christian Science Monitor
